posts.title: Hybrid Search: Fusing Keyword and Vector Retrieval
posts.subtitle: Dense embeddings miss exact terms; keyword search misses meaning — RAG systems that ship use both
posts.summary: Pure vector search embeds meaning but silently drops exact matches on IDs, error codes, and rare terms; pure keyword search (BM25) nails exact matches but misses paraphrases. Hybrid search runs both in parallel and merges the rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which needs no score normalization and is the default in production RAG stacks like Elasticsearch, Weaviate, and Azure AI Search.

slides.title: Two Retrievers, One Result List
slides.body: Hybrid search runs a lexical search (BM25) and a dense vector search over the same query at the same time, then merges the two ranked lists into one.
bullets: Standard in production RAG: Elasticsearch, Weaviate, Azure AI Search, and Vespa all ship a built-in hybrid mode
Not an ensemble of models — it's two different retrieval mechanisms scored and merged

slides.title: Vector Search Alone Has a Blind Spot
slides.body: Dense embeddings are trained to cluster semantically similar text, which is exactly why they struggle with tokens that carry no reusable meaning.
bullets: A query for error code 'ETIMEDOUT-4471' embeds close to other error messages in general, not to the one exact log line containing that string
Product SKUs, part numbers, proper nouns, and rare technical acronyms often get diluted into a generic 'technical text' region of embedding space
Embedding models are trained on general corpora — a term that never appeared in training data has no learned representation to anchor it precisely

slides.title: Keyword Search Alone Has the Opposite Blind Spot
slides.body: BM25 scores documents by term-frequency statistics — it counts matching words, it doesn't understand them.
bullets: A query for 'how do I stop my server from crashing under load' won't match a document that only says 'preventing OOM kills during traffic spikes' — zero shared keywords, same meaning
BM25 rewards exact term overlap, so paraphrases, synonyms, and cross-lingual matches score near zero regardless of relevance
This is precisely the gap vector search closes — the two methods fail on almost disjoint query types

slides.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: Merge Ranks, Not Scores
slides.body: BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores live on incomparable scales, so you can't just add them. RRF sidesteps that by using each result's RANK position instead of its raw score.
bullets: RRF formula: score(d) = sum over each ranked list of 1 / (k + rank(d)), with k typically 60
A document ranked #1 in BM25 and #3 in vector search gets 1/(60+1) + 1/(60+3) — no normalization, no tuning of relative weights required
Documents that appear in only one list still contribute, so a strong single-method match isn't discarded — it's just weighted lower than a document both methods agree on

slides.title: Worked Example: Two Lists Into One
slides.body: Query: 'reset password for API key 7f3a-node'. BM25 nails the exact token '7f3a-node'; the vector search nails the semantic intent of 'reset password'.
bullets: BM25 top-3: [Doc A: API key rotation guide (rank 1), Doc C: node config reference (rank 2), Doc B: password reset flow (rank 3)]
Vector top-3: [Doc B: password reset flow (rank 1), Doc D: account recovery overview (rank 2), Doc A: API key rotation guide (rank 3)]
RRF (k=60): Doc A = 1/61 + 1/63 ≈ 0.0323, Doc B = 1/63 + 1/61 ≈ 0.0323, Doc C ≈ 0.0161, Doc D ≈ 0.0159 — A and B tie for first, both promoted above single-method-only picks C and D

slides.title: When Each Method Wins
bullets: Numbers from BEIR-style retrieval benchmarks reported across Elastic, Weaviate, and Pinecone hybrid-search writeups — actual gains vary by corpus

rows: Typical recall@10 on mixed query sets

slides.title: Where It Costs More Than It's Worth
slides.body: Hybrid search isn't free — it roughly doubles retrieval-side infrastructure and adds a tuning parameter most teams skip.
bullets: You now maintain two indexes (an inverted index for BM25 and an ANN index like HNSW for vectors) instead of one, plus fusion logic
Latency is bounded by the slower of the two retrievers unless they run truly in parallel — a naive sequential implementation doubles p99

If your corpus is mostly natural-language prose with few exact identifiers (e.g. a novel's worth of narrative text), vector-only search captures nearly all the value and hybrid adds cost without much recall gain

slides.title: Default to Hybrid for Mixed-Content Corpora
slides.body: If your documents mix prose with identifiers, codes, names, or jargon — which most real knowledge bases do — hybrid search is the safer default, not an optimization to bolt on later.
bullets: BM25 catches exact terms; vector search catches meaning — hybrid catches both because it runs them in parallel, not as a fallback chain
RRF merges ranked lists without score normalization, using k≈60 as a stable, rarely-tuned default
Skip hybrid only when your corpus is near-pure natural language with few exact-match queries — otherwise the infrastructure cost buys real recall

questions.prompt: Why can't you just add raw BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores together to combine rankings?
options: You can — that's exactly what hybrid search does
The two scores live on incomparable scales, so a naive sum is dominated by whichever happens to have a larger numeric range
BM25 scores are always negative
Vector search doesn't produce a numeric score at all
questions.explanation: BM25 term-frequency scores and cosine-similarity scores have different, incomparable scales. Reciprocal Rank Fusion avoids this entirely by using each document's rank position rather than its raw score.

questions.prompt: In Reciprocal Rank Fusion, what happens to a document that appears in only one of the two ranked lists?
options: It is automatically discarded
It still contributes a score from that one list, just without a boost from the other
It automatically ranks #1
Fusion fails and falls back to BM25 only
questions.explanation: RRF sums 1/(k+rank) across whichever lists a document appears in. A single-list match still scores something — it's just typically lower than a document both retrievers agree on.

questions.prompt: A knowledge base is almost entirely narrative prose with very few exact identifiers or codes. What does the concept slide on tradeoffs suggest?
options: Hybrid search is always required regardless of content type
Vector-only search likely captures most of the value, and hybrid's added indexing/latency cost may not pay off
BM25-only is always better for prose
RRF's k parameter must be set to 0 in this case
questions.explanation: Hybrid search pays off most when a corpus mixes prose with exact-match terms (IDs, codes, jargon). For near-pure natural-language content with few exact-match queries, vector search alone often gets you most of the recall without doubling infrastructure.

posts.title: Consistent Hashing: Scaling Caches Without a Reshuffle
posts.subtitle: Add or remove one server and a naive hash remaps almost everything — consistent hashing remaps almost nothing
posts.summary: Naive modulo hashing (hash(key) % N) remaps roughly (N-1)/N of all keys whenever a server joins or leaves — catastrophic for a live cache. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on the same hash ring so only the keys adjacent to the changed server move, and virtual nodes fix the uneven-load problem that a plain ring introduces with few real servers.

slides.title: The Ring That Survives Scaling Events
slides.body: Consistent hashing maps both servers and keys onto the same circular hash space (a ring), so a key is owned by the first server found walking clockwise from its hash position.
bullets: Underpins Amazon DynamoDB, Apache Cassandra, Riak, and most distributed cache layers (Memcached client libraries, some CDN edge routing)
Solves one specific, painful problem: minimizing data movement when the set of servers changes

slides.title: Why hash(key) % N Falls Apart
slides.body: Modulo hashing is simple and perfectly balanced — until N changes, which is exactly when you need it most.
bullets: With 4 servers, key 'k' lives at hash(k) % 4. Scale to 5 servers and it's hash(k) % 5 — a completely different bucket for nearly every key
Adding or removing just one server out of N remaps roughly (N-1)/N of all keys — with 4 servers, that's about 75% of your entire cache invalidated at once
For a live cache, that means a massive simultaneous cache-miss stampede hitting the origin database right when you scaled specifically to handle more load

slides.title: Put Servers and Keys on the Same Ring
slides.body: Hash both server identifiers and keys into the same fixed space (e.g. 0 to 2^32-1), arranged as a circle. A key belongs to the next server clockwise from its position.
bullets: Removing a server only affects the keys that were mapped to it — they move to the next server clockwise, and nowhere else on the ring is touched
Adding a new server only steals keys from its immediate clockwise neighbor — every other server's key ownership is untouched
On average, adding or removing 1 of N servers now remaps only about 1/N of keys, not (N-1)/N

slides.title: The Catch: Uneven Load With Few Real Nodes
slides.body: A plain ring with only a handful of servers hashed to essentially random points produces lopsided arcs — one server can end up owning 50% of keyspace while another owns 5%.
bullets: With N=4 physical servers placed as single random points, the gaps between them on the ring are highly uneven purely by chance
A hot, oversized arc means that server takes disproportionate load and becomes the bottleneck — defeating the point of horizontal scaling
This is the classic failure mode people hit implementing 'textbook' consistent hashing with too few hash points

slides.title: Virtual Nodes Fix the Balance
slides.body: Instead of hashing each physical server to one point, hash it to many (typically 100-200) points scattered around the ring — called virtual nodes.
bullets: Each physical server now owns many small, scattered arcs instead of one large contiguous arc — the law of large numbers smooths out the imbalance
DynamoDB's original design uses this exact technique; Cassandra defaults to 256 virtual nodes (vnodes) per physical node
A bonus: when one server fails, its many small arcs redistribute across many other servers roughly evenly, instead of dumping the entire failed server's load onto just one clockwise neighbor

slides.title: Worked Example: Adding a 4th Cache Server
slides.body: 3 servers (A, B, C) hold keys on a ring. You add server D to handle growth.
bullets: Naive modulo (N: 3→4): virtually every key's bucket index changes — cache hit rate collapses to near 0% until it refills

Consistent hashing, no virtual nodes: D is inserted at one point on the ring and claims keys only from its immediate clockwise neighbor, say C — A and B's keys are completely untouched, only C's arc shrinks

Consistent hashing, 150 virtual nodes per server: D's 150 points scatter across the ring, each claiming a small slice from whichever server previously owned that point — total keys moved ≈ 1/4 of all keys (the theoretical minimum for going from 3 to 4 servers), spread evenly across A, B, and C rather than concentrated on one

slides.title: Modulo vs. Consistent Hashing

rows: Uneven without vnodes; even with ~100-200 vnodes/server

slides.title: Reach for the Ring When Membership Changes
slides.body: Consistent hashing is a targeted fix for one problem: minimizing data movement when nodes join or leave a distributed store.
bullets: If your server count is fixed and never changes, plain modulo hashing is simpler and equally well-balanced — don't add complexity you don't need
The moment you need to autoscale a cache/shard layer or tolerate node failures gracefully, consistent hashing turns a cluster-wide reshuffle into a local, partial one
Always pair it with virtual nodes (100+ per physical server) — a plain ring with too few real nodes routinely produces 2-5x load imbalance in practice

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of keys get remapped when you add one server to a cluster of N, using plain modulo hashing (hash(key) % N)?
options: About 1/N
About (N-1)/N — nearly all of them
Exactly 0
It depends only on the number of virtual nodes
questions.explanation: Because % N changes for almost every key when N changes, modulo hashing remaps roughly (N-1)/N of all keys on a single node addition or removal — for N=4, about 75%.

questions.prompt: What specific problem do virtual nodes solve in consistent hashing?
options: They make the hash function cryptographically secure
They fix the load imbalance caused by a small number of physical servers landing at uneven, random points on the ring
They eliminate the need for a hash ring entirely
They reduce the total number of keys that need to be stored
questions.explanation: With only a handful of real servers hashed to single random points, the arcs between them are highly uneven by chance, causing lopsided load. Giving each server 100-200 virtual points smooths this out via the law of large numbers.

questions.prompt: When a server fails in a ring that uses 150 virtual nodes per physical server, what happens to its load?
options: All of it dumps onto exactly one other server
It's lost until the server is manually reassigned
It redistributes across many other servers roughly evenly, since the failed server's arcs were scattered across the ring
The entire ring must be rebuilt from scratch
questions.explanation: Because each physical server owns many small, scattered arcs (via its virtual nodes) rather than one contiguous arc, a failure spreads its former load across many neighbors instead of overloading a single one.

posts.title: Claude Fable 5.1: Same Model, Two Safety Tiers
posts.subtitle: Anthropic doubled a science benchmark score and cut cache pricing 75% — but the real cost story is more complicated
posts.summary: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 more than doubles Fable 5's score on Terminal-Bench-Science while Claude Mythos 5.1 — the identical model under different safeguards — targets cybersecurity and life-sciences work. Cache-read pricing dropped 75%, but independent testing found Fable 5.1 burns ~1.7x more output tokens per task, so cheaper rates don't automatically mean cheaper bills.

slides.title: Same Model, Two Safety Tiers
slides.body: On September 1, 2026, Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 — described as its most advanced models yet for coding and knowledge work.
bullets: Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 are the same underlying model with different safeguard configurations
Fable 5.1 is generally available now; Mythos 5.1 ships only through Anthropic's trusted-access programs

slides.title: Fable 5 Was Losing Ground on Real Scientific Work
slides.body: Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 tests multi-step research tasks — reading papers, running computations, drawing conclusions — not trivia recall.
bullets: Fable 5 scored 24.7% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 — below Opus 5's 29.0%, roughly level with GPT-5.6 Sol's 22.4%
The gap showed up specifically at higher effort tiers, where longer, multi-step reasoning chains compound small errors
A model billed as a knowledge-work tool was underperforming on exactly the workflows knowledge workers run

slides.title: More Than Double, Concentrated at High Effort
slides.body: Fable 5.1 matches or beats Fable 5 at low/medium effort, and pulls far ahead once you turn the effort dial up.
bullets: 52.6% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 — more than double Fable 5's 24.7%, and well past Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol
55.8% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 versus 42.0% for Fable 5
Anthropic attributes the jump to higher-effort reasoning tiers, not a change at the low-effort default setting

slides.title: The Benchmark Table
bullets: Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 grades real research workflows; scores are self-reported by Anthropic

slides.title: Mythos 5.1: Same Weights, Different Leash
slides.body: Mythos 5.1 isn't a separate model trained for security work — it's Fable 5.1 released with safeguards built for cybersecurity and life-sciences use.
bullets: Available only through Anthropic's trusted-access programs, not the general API
Its cybersecurity safeguards trigger 60% fewer false positives than the prior safeguard generation
It can identify and describe a software vulnerability but is specifically blocked from producing a working exploit for it

slides.title: A Security Team's Actual Workflow
slides.body: A security engineer under trusted access points Mythos 5.1 at a batch of flagged CVEs in an open-source parsing library.
bullets: The model correctly identifies a memory-safety bug and explains the flawed bounds check causing it
Asked to write a proof-of-concept exploit chain, it refuses — vulnerability discovery is in scope, exploit development is not
The fewer-false-positives improvement means the triage list the engineer reviews is shorter and more trustworthy than before

slides.title: The Catch: Cheaper Rate Card, Pricier Task
slides.body: Input/output pricing didn't move — it's still $10 / $50 per million tokens. The only listed cut is cache reads: $1 down to $0.25 per million tokens, a 75% reduction.
bullets: That cache-read cut is why Anthropic quotes 25% cheaper for typical workloads and up to 45% for highly agentic ones that reuse context heavily
Independent testing from Artificial Analysis found Fable 5.1 uses roughly 1.7x more output tokens to solve the same task as Fable 5
Net effect: cost per completed task can end up higher than Fable 5 despite the cheaper cache rate — the rate card and the bill are not the same number

slides.title: Before You Switch, Benchmark Your Own Bill
slides.body: A rate-card cut and a workload-cost cut are different claims, and this release ships both — pointing in different directions.
bullets: Fable 5.1 is a real jump on high-effort, multi-step reasoning — not a marginal update
Mythos 5.1 shows Anthropic decoupling capability from access: same weights, gated differently for sensitive domains
Don't trust the headline discount — measure output-token volume on your actual tasks before assuming a cheaper cache rate means a cheaper bill

They are the same underlying model with different safeguard configurations and access tiers
Mythos 5.1 is an older, cheaper version of Fable 5.1
They share no relationship — separate models from separate teams

Only on tasks under 100 tokens

options: Input token pricing also increased
Independent testing found it uses roughly 1.7x more output tokens to solve the same task
The cache-read cut only applies to Mythos 5.1
Fable 5.1 requires twice as many API calls per request
questions.explanation: Artificial Analysis found Fable 5.1 generates about 1.7x more output tokens per task than Fable 5. Since only cache-read pricing dropped — not output pricing — heavier output usage can offset or exceed the cache savings.

posts.title: VoiceMem: Giving Voice AI Two Separate Memories
posts.subtitle: A streaming 'dual-brain' architecture splits facts from feelings so speech models can remember a caller without adding latency
posts.summary: VoiceMem (NTU Singapore, NUS, Tsinghua, CUHK) retrofits duplex speech language models with an explicit two-part memory — a factual 'left brain' and an emotional 'right brain' — using distillation rather than retraining. It beats Mem0-style retrieval by ~30 points and completes lookups in 134ms, fast enough not to add conversational delay.

slides.title: Two Brains for One Voice
slides.body: VoiceMem gives real-time, duplex speech language models something they've lacked: an explicit, queryable memory — split the way memory is split in biology.
bullets: From NTU Singapore, NUS, Tsinghua University, and CUHK
Built on top of existing speech models: Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, and Step-Audio2-Mini

slides.title: Voice Assistants Forget Mid-Call
slides.body: Duplex speech LMs stream audio in and text/audio out directly, with no persistent store for what was said or how the caller felt about it.
bullets: Text-first memory systems like Mem0 don't fit a streaming audio pipeline built for turn-by-turn latency, not periodic text retrieval
Without memory, an assistant can't recall a fact from 10 minutes earlier in the same call, let alone across calls
Emotional/relationship context — that a caller was already frustrated — gets dropped entirely between turns

slides.title: Split Memory Like a Brain
slides.body: VoiceMem uses two separate memory stores instead of one blended vector index.
bullets: Left brain: factual, episodic memory — names, dates, stated preferences — retrieved by top-k similarity search
Right brain: affective/persona memory tracking emotional state and relationship history across turns
Cross-brain associations link specific facts to the emotional context they were said in, so retrieval can pull both together

slides.title: No Architecture Surgery Needed
slides.body: Instead of retraining a speech model from scratch, VoiceMem converts an existing one via online black-box on-policy distillation.
bullets: A teacher model supervises the student on its own generated rollouts — no need to see or modify the student's internals
Applied to Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, and Step-Audio2-Mini, all originally speech-input/text-output only
Result: the first speech language models with explicit, queryable memory access, without a from-scratch retrain

slides.title: The Numbers
bullets: Baseline comparisons are against classical retrieval systems and prior best persona-tracking systems

rows: Top-5 retrieval accuracy, top-200 candidate pool

slides.title: The Allergy and the Attitude
slides.body: A caller mentions early on they're allergic to shellfish and sounds frustrated about a delayed order.
bullets: 20 minutes later they ask for restaurant recommendations
The left brain recalls the allergy and filters it out of suggestions automatically

The right brain keeps the assistant's tone measured, because it tracked the earlier frustration — all retrieved in 134ms, comfortably inside standard voice-activity-detection latency windows, so the reply doesn't stall

slides.title: Where It Doesn't Help
slides.body: 134ms retrieval and dual-brain tracking are overhead you pay on every turn — worth it only when continuity actually matters.
bullets: Single-shot Q&A bots with no need for cross-turn continuity gain nothing and just pay the extra compute
Quality is bounded by the teacher model used in distillation — a weak teacher caps what the student can learn
Evaluated only on the open Qwen/Step-Audio2 family; generalization to closed real-time systems (e.g. ChatGPT Realtime, Gemini Live) is untested

slides.title: Facts and Feelings Need Separate Stores
slides.body: VoiceMem's core bet is architectural: one memory store trying to hold both facts and affect underperforms two specialized ones with a bridge between them.
bullets: Splitting factual and affective memory outperforms a single blended store on both fronts
Distillation, not retraining, is enough to retrofit memory onto an existing speech LM
134ms is the number that decides whether memory feels instant or makes a voice assistant visibly pause

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a text-first memory system like Mem0 fit well into a duplex speech language model?
options: Mem0 requires GPUs that speech models don't use
It's built around periodic text retrieval, not the turn-by-turn latency constraints of a streaming audio pipeline
Mem0 only works with images, not text or audio
Speech models can't call any external memory store
questions.explanation: Duplex speech LMs stream audio in and out under tight latency budgets. Text-first memory systems weren't designed for that constraint, which is part of why VoiceMem builds a memory system natively streamed alongside the audio.

questions.prompt: What does VoiceMem's 'dual-brain' split actually separate?
options: Input audio from output audio
Factual/episodic memory from affective/persona memory
Short conversations from long conversations
English from other languages
questions.explanation: The 'left brain' holds facts (names, dates, preferences) while the 'right brain' tracks emotional state and relationship history, with cross-brain associations linking the two.

questions.prompt: How did the authors turn existing speech-input/text-output models into memory-augmented speech LMs?
options: By pretraining new models from scratch on memory-labeled data
By manually editing the models' attention layers to add memory heads
Via online black-box on-policy distillation from a teacher model, without architectural surgery
By fine-tuning only on text, then converting to audio afterward
questions.explanation: VoiceMem uses a teacher model to supervise the student on its own rollouts (on-policy distillation), treating the student as a black box — no need to modify its internal architecture.

posts.title: MCP Goes Stateless: Why Sessions Left the Protocol
posts.subtitle: The 2026-07-28 spec deletes the handshake and the session header — turning MCP servers into ordinary, load-balancer-friendly HTTP workloads
posts.summary: MCP's 2026-07-28 spec revision removes the initialize handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header, making every request self-contained (SEP-2567). Roots, Sampling, and Logging are deprecated alongside it (SEP-2577) because they assumed a session existed to hang capability negotiation on — a 12-month window keeps old servers working while new ones move to per-request scope.

slides.title: MCP Just Stopped Remembering You Between Calls
slides.body: The 2026-07-28 MCP specification makes the protocol core stateless: no session ID, no per-connection handshake — every request now carries everything a server needs to answer it.
bullets: Ships as SEP-2567 in the 2026-07-28 spec revision
Official TypeScript, Python, Go, and C# SDKs already support it; Rust support is in beta

slides.title: Sessions Don't Survive Being Load-Balanced
slides.body: The original MCP transport opened with an initialize/initialized handshake, then tracked the connection via an Mcp-Session-Id header.
bullets: That meant a load balancer needed sticky routing — same client always hitting the same server instance — or a shared session store across replicas
Scaling an MCP server horizontally meant re-solving the same problem stateful web apps hit decades earlier
A protocol pitched as lightweight infrastructure was carrying session-affinity requirements most HTTP APIs don't have

slides.title: SEP-2567: Delete the Handshake, Not the Protocol
slides.body: The fix wasn't a patch — it removed session state from the transport entirely.
bullets: initialize/initialized and the Mcp-Session-Id header are gone from the 2026-07-28 core spec
Every request is a single, self-contained HTTP POST carrying its own protocol version, client identity, and capabilities
Streamable HTTP moves to one POST per message instead of a long-lived stream tied to a session

slides.title: Any Request, Any Instance, No Coordination
slides.body: Because no request depends on a prior one, any server instance behind a plain round-robin load balancer can answer any request.
bullets: Sticky sessions and shared session stores are no longer required at the protocol layer
An MCP server becomes an ordinary HTTP workload — deployable as a serverless function (request in, response out) instead of a long-running process
Version and capability negotiation moves from a one-time handshake to per-request headers, checked on every call

slides.title: Before vs. After

rows: Sticky routing or shared session store

slides.title: What Got Deprecated Alongside Sessions
slides.body: SEP-2577 deprecates Roots, Sampling, and Logging in the same revision — all three assumed a stateful session existed to hang capability negotiation on.
bullets: They keep working for a 12-month deprecation window, but new servers shouldn't build on them
Roots — letting a client hand a server a filesystem scope once, at connect time — is the clearest example
Its replacement: pass that scope explicitly as a tool parameter, resource URI, or plain config on each call, instead of negotiating it once per session

slides.title: What This Breaks in Practice
slides.body: Statelessness at the protocol layer doesn't mean your server logic gets simpler for free — it means you can't lean on the transport to remember things for you anymore.
bullets: Any server that cached per-session state in memory — auth context, negotiated capabilities, an open Roots list — now has to re-derive or re-pass it on every request
Mixed-SDK deployments can hit version mismatches while Rust support is still in beta and others are already stable
A server that keeps relying on Roots/Sampling/Logging past the 12-month window simply stops being called by newer clients — there's no hard cutover date to miss, just a quiet compatibility cliff

slides.title: Statelessness Is a Scaling Decision
slides.body: This is the same tradeoff HTTP itself made over stateful RPC, applied to an AI-tooling protocol a few years after it needed to scale.
bullets: Moving state out of the transport and into each request payload is what lets a server be served by any instance behind a load balancer
If you operate an MCP server, audit for anything you assumed persisted across a session before migrating
Roots, Sampling, and Logging still work today — but building new integrations on them is building on a 12-month clock

questions.prompt: What specifically does SEP-2567 remove from the MCP protocol core?
options: All tool-calling functionality
The initialize/initialized handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header
Support for HTTP entirely, in favor of raw sockets
The ability to use resources
questions.explanation: SEP-2567 removes the connection handshake and session header, making each request a self-contained unit that carries its own protocol version, identity, and capabilities.

questions.prompt: Why did removing session state help MCP servers scale horizontally?
options: It made requests smaller, reducing bandwidth
Because no request depends on a prior one, any server instance can answer any request without sticky routing or a shared session store
It added a caching layer that speeds up repeated requests
It requires fewer SDKs to maintain
questions.explanation: Stateless requests remove the need for a load balancer to route a client to the same instance every time, or for replicas to share a session store — any instance can serve any request.

questions.prompt: What replaces the deprecated Roots primitive under the 2026-07-28 spec?
options: Nothing — filesystem access is no longer possible via MCP
A new, more complex session-negotiation step
Passing the scope explicitly as a tool parameter, resource URI, or plain config on each call
A dedicated Roots-only server process
questions.explanation: Since Roots relied on negotiating a filesystem scope once per session, and sessions are gone, the replacement is to pass that scope explicitly with each request instead of relying on a one-time handshake.

posts.title: Random Attention: Deleting KV Cache Entries at Random
posts.subtitle: A signal-free eviction rule that matches learned selectors and serves faster.
posts.summary: Salesforce AI Research's Random Attention evicts KV cache entries uniformly at random instead of scoring them, matching learned selectors like SnapKV and TriAttention on reasoning benchmarks while serving 32-43% faster in vLLM.

slides.title: The KV Cache Is Reasoning's New Bottleneck
slides.body: Reasoning models like Qwen3 and Phi-4-reasoning write chains of thought that run tens of thousands of tokens long before answering — and every one of those tokens has to stay in GPU memory as a key/value pair.
bullets: A 32B model reasoning through a 32K-token chain of thought can burn more memory on its KV cache than on its own weights
That memory ceiling caps how many requests a server can batch at once

slides.title: Existing Fixes All Try to Score Tokens First
slides.body: Prior KV-cache eviction methods (SnapKV, R-KV, VaSE, TriAttention) keep the cache small by scoring every token for predicted future importance and evicting the low scorers.
bullets: Scoring means extra attention passes over the cache on every eviction round
Some methods (TriAttention) also need per-model calibration data collected in advance
None of that scoring machinery is free — it costs compute and latency exactly where you're trying to save both

slides.title: Keep the Prompt, Evict the Rest Uniformly at Random
slides.body: Random Attention never evicts a single prompt token — the prompt is the one place unique information lives. For everything the model has generated since, it keeps a uniformly random subset per attention head up to a fixed budget, plus a short window of the most recent tokens.
bullets: No attention scores computed, no calibration data collected — an eviction round costs only the memory compaction itself
The insight: a chain of thought re-derives and restates the same facts many times, so which repetitions survive matters less than how many tokens survive
Tested on Qwen3-4B/14B/32B and Phi-4-reasoning across MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, AIME, HMMT, and LiveCodeBench

slides.title: Matches Scored Selectors, Serves Meaningfully Faster
slides.body: At matched KV budgets, Random Attention's accuracy ties or beats every scored baseline the authors tested — and it's the fastest evictor in both their Hugging Face harness and a vLLM serving stack.
bullets: Reported 32-43% higher throughput than the strongest scored evictor when served in vLLM

slides.title: Worked Example: A 24K-Token Competition Math Problem
slides.body: Picture Qwen3-32B tackling an AIME-style problem. By token 20,000 of its chain of thought, the KV cache under a fixed budget holds: the entire original prompt, a random ~10% sample of everything reasoned so far, and a short window of the most recent tokens.
bullets: No token was kept because it scored as 'important' — it survived by chance
The final answer still comes out right because the key algebraic steps got restated multiple times earlier in the trace, so losing any one restatement doesn't erase the fact from the cache

slides.title: When This Wouldn't Hold Up
slides.body: The result is specific to reasoning traces, where redundancy is the norm — it's not a general claim that scoring is useless.
bullets: A single fact mentioned exactly once deep in a long context (classic 'needle in a haystack' retrieval) has no redundancy to fall back on if randomly evicted
The paper's guarantees are benchmarked on math/science/code reasoning tasks — not on long-document QA or multi-turn chat memory
The prompt itself is never evicted precisely because it isn't redundant like the generated trace is

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Before building a learned scorer, test whether a dumb random baseline already gets you most of the way there — here it matched or beat four scored methods
Removing the scoring step doesn't just simplify the system, it removes a real cost: 32-43% more throughput in vLLM serving
The trick only works because reasoning chains are redundant by nature — don't assume it transfers to tasks where information appears exactly once

questions.prompt: What does Random Attention actually keep in the KV cache?
options: Only the most recent N tokens
The full prompt, plus a uniformly random subset of generated tokens and a short recency window
Tokens with the highest attention scores
Tokens chosen by a small calibration model trained per-model
questions.explanation: Unlike scored evictors, it computes no importance scores at all. It always preserves the full prompt, then keeps a random per-head sample of the generated tokens plus a short window near the current position.

questions.prompt: Why does random eviction hold up almost as well as learned scoring specifically on reasoning traces?
options: Reasoning chains restate and re-derive the same facts many times, so losing any single repetition rarely erases the information
Attention scores are mathematically incorrect
GPUs cannot compute attention scores fast enough to matter
The paper only tested traces shorter than 500 tokens
questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought text is redundant by nature — the same intermediate facts get restated as the model reasons forward. That redundancy is exactly what a needle-in-a-haystack task lacks, which is why this result doesn't automatically generalize there.

questions.prompt: What's the main efficiency win from skipping token scoring entirely?
options: It needs no extra attention computation or calibration data, so an eviction round costs only compaction
It eliminates the need for a KV cache altogether
It reduces the model's parameter count
It guarantees higher accuracy on every task
questions.explanation: Scored evictors spend extra compute ranking cached tokens (and sometimes running calibration passes). Random Attention skips that step entirely, which the authors measured as 32-43% higher throughput than the strongest scored baseline in vLLM.

references.title: Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning (arXiv:2609.03430)

posts.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash: More Thinking, Same Sticker Price
posts.subtitle: Google's third Flash model in six weeks trades tokens for reliability, not size.
posts.summary: Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash, released September 2, 2026, is the same base model as 3.7 Flash retrained to spend more compute per task — jumping from 81.6% to 90.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 at the same introductory price, alongside a safeguarded Cyber variant for vulnerability discovery.

slides.title: Google Ships Its Third Flash Model in Six Weeks
slides.body: Gemini 3.8 Flash launched September 2, 2026 — not a bigger model, but the same 3.7 Flash checkpoint lineage tuned to work harder on every request.
bullets: Available immediately in the Gemini app, AI Mode, Google Sheets, Antigravity, AI Studio, and the Gemini API

slides.title: 3.7 Flash Was Fast, But Shallow on Hard Tasks
slides.body: Flash models exist to trade some capability for speed and cost. That trade started showing on long-horizon software engineering, multi-step agentic work, and specialized-domain reasoning, where 3.7 Flash lagged frontier-tier models.
bullets: Closing that gap by simply shipping a bigger model would break Flash's cost promise
Google needed a way to buy more reliability without changing the price tier

slides.title: Same Weights, Tuned to Spend More Effort
slides.body: Gemini 3.8 Flash is built on the same underlying model as 3.7 Flash, but trained to be more diligent: at higher 'effort' settings it runs extra reasoning steps and calls tools iteratively instead of stopping after the first pass.
bullets: Effort level is a developer-facing dial, not a fixed behavior
This is an inference-time compute trade, not a bigger network

slides.title: The Terminal-Bench Jump Is the Headline Number
bullets: Google also introduced Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, a safeguarded variant for trusted testers under a new 'Fairwind' access program, reported to find real vulnerabilities in a majority of Google's internal discovery evaluation cases

slides.title: Worked Example: A Multi-File Refactor
slides.body: Ask an agent to refactor a feature spanning several files and fix whatever tests break. At a low effort setting, 3.8 Flash behaves like 3.7 Flash — one pass, done. Dial effort up, and it re-runs the test suite after its own edits, catches a regression, and iterates before returning control.
bullets: That extra verification loop is the 'diligence' Google is describing, not a change in what the model knows

slides.title: The Catch: Same Price Per Token, Not Same Cost Per Task
slides.body: Gemini 3.8 Flash matches 3.7 Flash's introductory price — $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens — through December 31, 2026, rising to $1.50/$7.50 after.
bullets: Higher effort means more reasoning and tool-call tokens per request, so a workload's total bill can rise even though the per-token rate didn't
Teams should set effort deliberately: low for simple, high-volume tasks; high only where the extra verification is worth paying for

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: 3.8 Flash is a 'try harder' upgrade to 3.7 Flash's same base model, not a new larger model
The reported jump — 81.6% to 90.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 — comes from extra reasoning and tool-call steps at higher effort, not new weights
Pricing per token is unchanged short-term, but real workload cost scales with effort level, so tune it per task rather than maxing it out by default
The gated Cyber variant signals a broader industry pattern: safety-critical model capabilities increasingly ship to a restricted access tier first, not a public API

questions.prompt: What is the core technical change from Gemini 3.7 Flash to 3.8 Flash?
options: A much larger set of model weights
The same base model, tuned to spend more inference compute and effort per task
A switch from a transformer to a diffusion architecture
Removal of tool-calling support to cut latency
questions.explanation: Google describes 3.8 Flash as the same model lineage as 3.7 Flash, trained to execute more reasoning steps and call tools iteratively — especially at higher developer-set effort levels — rather than being a bigger network.

questions.prompt: On which reported benchmark did Google highlight the largest jump, and by how much?
options: Terminal-Bench 2.1, from 81.6% to 90.8%
ImageNet classification, from 50% to 90%
MMLU, from 99% to 100%
No benchmark showed improvement
questions.explanation: Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluates agentic, terminal-based tasks — exactly the long-horizon, tool-using workloads 3.8 Flash was tuned to handle more diligently.

questions.prompt: Why might a team's total inference bill rise even though 3.8 Flash's per-token price matches 3.7 Flash's introductory rate?
options: Because 3.8 Flash spends more tokens per task at higher effort settings
Because Google doubled the context window limit
Because using the Cyber variant is now mandatory
Because pricing moved from per-token to per-request billing
questions.explanation: Effort is a dial, not a discount — running more reasoning steps and tool calls per request means more billed tokens per task, even at an unchanged per-token price.

posts.title: Agent Memory: Giving AI Agents a Past
posts.subtitle: A long context window is not the same thing as remembering anything.
posts.summary: Context windows are bounded and reset; memory is a separate system that persists facts and history across sessions. Splitting memory into working, episodic, and semantic layers lets agents recall what happened and what's currently true without re-reading everything, every time.

slides.title: An Agent's Context Window Is Not Its Memory
slides.body: A coding agent that runs across days of work, or a support agent handling the same customer for months, needs state that survives well past any single context window.
bullets: Even a 1M-token window is bounded, expensive to fill, and gone the moment a new session starts

slides.title: Stuffing Everything Into the Prompt Doesn't Scale
slides.body: The naive fix — replay the full transcript every turn — breaks down well before you hit the token limit.
bullets: Cost and latency grow every single turn as the transcript grows
Long prompts dilute attention: models reliably lose instructions buried in the middle of a long context
Some facts (a user's preferences, a codebase's conventions) need to persist across sessions entirely — they were never 'in' this session's transcript to replay

slides.title: Three Layers: Working, Episodic, Semantic
slides.body: A common pattern splits agent memory by how long it needs to live and how it's retrieved.
bullets: Working memory — the live context window: the current task, recent turns, nothing more

Episodic memory — a log of what happened, usually in a vector store or structured file, retrieved by similarity or recency (a coding agent's own 'progress.md' between sessions is a simple version of this)
Semantic memory — distilled, standing facts extracted from episodes: a user profile, a project's house style, a persistent 'CLAUDE.md'-style conventions file

slides.title: Worked Example: A Refactor Spanning Three Sessions
slides.body: Session 1: the agent explores an unfamiliar codebase and writes its findings to a memory file. Session 2 starts with a completely empty context window, but reads that file first and skips re-exploring from scratch.
bullets: In session 3 the user corrects a wrong assumption the agent made — the fix goes into the semantic memory, not just that session's transcript
Session 4 inherits the correction automatically, without anyone re-explaining it

slides.title: Picking a Strategy Trades Cost Against Persistence

rows: Hits context limit, gets slow and expensive
Distillation loses nuance or goes stale

slides.title: When Memory Helps vs. When It Hurts
bullets: Stale memory is worse than no memory: a 'fact' that was true last month but isn't now can mislead an agent with full confidence — memories need expiry or versioning, not just storage
Retrieval-based episodic memory adds latency and can inject irrelevant context — a smaller version of the same 'lost in the middle' problem
For short, single-session tasks, a memory system is pure overhead — plain context is simpler and just as effective
Long-term memory writes are an attack surface: a prompt injection that tricks an agent into writing a false 'fact' can persist and mislead every future session

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Memory is a separate storage-and-retrieval system with its own write/read/expiry policy — it is not 'a bigger context window'
Match the layer to the lifespan: working memory for the current task, episodic for what happened, semantic for what's now true
Always give memory a path to correction or expiry, or the agent will repeat old mistakes with total confidence

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between an agent's context window and its memory system?
options: There is no real difference — they're the same mechanism
The context window is bounded, live working state for the current session; memory is separate storage designed to persist and be retrieved across sessions
Memory is always computed faster than reading the context window
Context windows can never run out of space
questions.explanation: The context window resets with every new session and is expensive to keep full. Memory systems exist precisely to carry state past that boundary.

questions.prompt: In the working/episodic/semantic memory model, what is 'semantic memory'?
options: A raw, complete log of every past message
Distilled, compact facts or preferences pulled from past interactions, like a user profile or a project's conventions
The model's frozen weights
A cache that stores embeddings but is never read by the agent
questions.explanation: Semantic memory holds standing facts extracted from episodes — the kind of thing you'd write once into a conventions file rather than re-derive from a transcript every session.

questions.prompt: Why can stale memory be worse than having no memory at all?
options: It takes up extra disk space
It can silently and confidently mislead the agent with information that used to be true but no longer is
It always causes the agent to crash
It has no meaningful downside
questions.explanation: An agent with no memory has no false assumption to act on. An agent with a stale memory acts on outdated 'facts' with the same confidence as current ones — and that false confidence compounds across future turns.

posts.title: GigaPath-Flash: 50x Cheaper Pathology Foundation Models
posts.subtitle: Distilling a billion-parameter pathology model into ~43M parameters keeps 97% of the accuracy at 1/50th the compute.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research's GigaPath-Flash distills the billion-parameter GigaPath pathology model into a 43M-parameter pair of encoders, keeping 97% of predictive performance at roughly 50x less compute. Its sibling GigaTIME-Flash runs 6x faster and uses 8x less memory, making population-scale slide analysis feasible on a single GPU.

slides.title: 50x Cheaper Pathology AI, 97% of the Accuracy
slides.body: Microsoft Research shrank a billion-parameter pathology foundation model down to ~43M parameters — and kept almost all of its predictive power.

slides.title: A Single Slide Is a Billion Pixels
slides.body: Whole-slide pathology images routinely exceed a gigapixel. Running a foundation model on even one slide means processing thousands of image tiles — and that cost multiplies fast.
bullets: One whole-slide image (WSI) = thousands of tiles fed through a tile encoder
The original GigaPath uses a ~1B-parameter ViT-g tile encoder
At tens of thousands of patients, compute cost becomes the bottleneck for discovery, not data availability

slides.title: Distill the Teacher, Keep Two Small Encoders
slides.body: GigaPath-Flash distills the original GigaPath ViT-g teacher into a 22M-parameter ViT-S tile encoder, then aggregates tiles with a 21M-parameter LongNet slide encoder that uses dilated attention to scale to huge tile counts without quadratic blowup.
bullets: 22M-param ViT-S tile encoder, distilled from the 1B-param ViT-g teacher
21M-param LongNet slide encoder (dilated attention, not full self-attention, across tiles)
~43M total params — about 50x smaller than the original GigaPath
GigaTIME-Flash reuses the same ViT-S backbone plus a lightweight conv decoder, fine-tuned with LoRA, for H&E-to-multiplex-immunofluorescence translation

slides.title: The Efficiency Trade Holds Up
slides.body: Both Flash models trade a small accuracy gap for a large compute win — and on some out-of-distribution cohorts, GigaTIME-Flash actually matches or beats the original.

slides.title: Scaling to a Million Slides on One GPU
slides.body: The compute savings compound directly into wall-clock time for population-scale studies — the exact regime where the original model was impractical.
bullets: 1,000 slides: ~2 GPU-hours with GigaTIME-Flash vs. ~7 GPU-hours with GigaTIME
100,000 slides: ~7 GPU-days vs. ~30 GPU-days
1,000,000 slides: ~70 GPU-days vs. ~300 GPU-days
GigaPath-Flash also processes over 1,600 tiles/sec at batch size 128

slides.title: Efficient Isn't the Same as Validated
slides.body: Microsoft Research is explicit that this is an early research release, not a clinical tool — the efficiency gains don't skip the validation step.
bullets: Evaluations so far cover a limited set of benchmarks and cohorts (PANDA prostate grading, EBRAINS brain tumor subtyping)
Broader validation across tasks, scanners, and patient populations is still needed
Downstream clinical use requires multi-institutional, prospective validation — not just a benchmark score
Distillation trades a small, real accuracy gap (97%, not 100%) for a 50x compute win — fine for large-scale discovery, riskier for a single high-stakes diagnosis

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Distillation can shrink a foundation model 50x in compute while keeping ~97% of its accuracy
Dilated (LongNet) attention lets a slide encoder aggregate thousands of tiles without quadratic cost
Compute reduction turns population-scale analysis (millions of slides) from a cluster job into a single-GPU job
An efficient model is still a research release until it clears multi-institutional clinical validation

questions.prompt: How does GigaPath-Flash shrink its tile encoder from ~1B parameters to 22M?
options: Post-training quantization to 8-bit weights
Knowledge distillation from the original GigaPath ViT-g teacher
Pruning attention heads after training
Reducing the input tile resolution
questions.explanation: Distillation transfers the representational capacity of the large teacher model into a much smaller student, rather than compressing the teacher's own weights directly.

questions.prompt: What lets GigaPath-Flash's slide encoder aggregate thousands of tiles from a gigapixel image efficiently?
options: A recurrent LSTM run over tile order
LongNet's dilated attention
Fixed-size average pooling of all tiles
Cropping every slide down to a fixed tile count
questions.explanation: Dilated attention lets the slide encoder attend across huge tile counts without the quadratic cost of full self-attention over every tile pair.

questions.prompt: According to Microsoft Research, what is still required before these models could be used clinically?
options: Nothing — they are already validated for clinical deployment
Multi-institutional, prospective validation across scanners and populations
A bigger teacher model to distill from
Replacing the slide encoder with a Transformer-XL
questions.explanation: The release is explicit that it's an early research release: broader validation across tasks, scanners, and patient populations is still needed before any clinical use.

references.title: GigaPath-Flash and GigaTIME-Flash: Toward population-scale discovery with efficient pathology foundation models — Microsoft Research

posts.title: Sliding Window Attention: Local Focus, Global Reach
posts.subtitle: Cap every token's attention to a fixed nearby window, then let depth or hybrid layers carry information the rest of the way.
posts.summary: Full self-attention costs grow quadratically with sequence length, which breaks down for long context. Sliding window attention caps each token's attention to a fixed nearby window, cutting cost to linear in sequence length — and models recover long-range reach either by stacking layers (Mistral 7B) or alternating local windows with full-attention layers (Gemma 2).

slides.title: Local Focus, Global Reach
slides.body: Full attention lets every token see every other token — at a quadratic price. Sliding window attention trades some of that reach for speed.

slides.title: Full Attention Doesn't Scale
slides.body: In standard self-attention, every token computes a score against every other token, so cost grows as O(n^2) with sequence length n.
bullets: Doubling the context length roughly quadruples the attention compute and memory
For a 100,000-token sequence, that's on the order of 10 billion pairwise attention scores per layer
This is the core wall that makes very long context expensive to serve, not just to train

slides.title: Cap Attention to a Fixed-Size Window
slides.body: Instead of attending to all n tokens, each token only attends to the w nearest tokens on either side. Cost drops from O(n^2) to O(n * w) — linear in sequence length.
bullets: Typical window sizes: 512-4096 tokens, depending on the model
For a 100,000-token sequence with window w=4096, that's about 410 million pairwise scores instead of 10 billion — roughly 24x fewer
The catch: a single layer can no longer connect two tokens that are farther apart than the window

slides.title: Two Ways to Recover Long-Range Info
slides.body: Losing direct long-range attention in one layer doesn't mean losing it entirely — models recover it either through depth or through hybrid layers.

rows: A handful of tokens get 'global attention' to/from everything
Receptive field compounds with depth across 32 layers

slides.title: Stacking Layers to Widen the Reach
slides.body: In a pure sliding-window stack like Mistral 7B's, token A in layer 1 only sees tokens within 4096 positions. But layer 2 attends to layer-1 outputs, which already encode information from their own local windows — so the effective receptive field compounds with each added layer.
bullets: Layer 1: each token's representation reflects its immediate 4096-token window
Layer 2: attending within a 4096-token window now reaches information that already traveled up to 4096 tokens further in layer 1
After enough layers, the theoretical reach can span well beyond the raw window size — without ever computing a full n x n attention matrix

slides.title: When Windows Miss the Point
slides.body: Cheaper attention isn't free — it changes what the model can do in a single hop, and that has real failure modes.
bullets: Pure local windows can struggle with 'needle in a haystack' tasks that need a precise, single-hop link between two distant tokens
If depth isn't sufficient to compound the receptive field, relevant context outside the window is effectively invisible to that layer
Hybrid designs (local + periodic global layers) trade back some of the compute savings to guarantee long-range access
Window size becomes another hyperparameter to tune against your task's actual dependency distance

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Full self-attention costs O(n^2); sliding window attention costs O(n * w), linear in sequence length
A single sliding-window layer can't directly connect tokens farther apart than the window
Models recover long-range reach either by stacking depth (Mistral 7B) or mixing in periodic global-attention layers (Gemma 2, Longformer)
The tradeoff shows up as a real limitation on tasks needing precise long-distance retrieval in shallow networks

questions.prompt: Why does full self-attention become expensive for long sequences?
options: It requires more GPU memory bandwidth per token than any other layer type
Its cost grows quadratically (O(n^2)) with sequence length
It can only run on TPUs, not GPUs
It requires retraining the tokenizer for every new sequence length
questions.explanation: Every token scores against every other token, so the number of pairwise computations scales with n^2 — doubling sequence length roughly quadruples the cost.

questions.prompt: In a pure sliding-window design like Mistral 7B's (no global layers), how does information from far-away tokens reach a given position?
options: It doesn't — those tokens are permanently inaccessible
By stacking layers, so the effective receptive field compounds with depth
Through a separate retrieval index bolted onto the model
By periodically resetting the window to cover the full sequence
questions.explanation: Each layer's window reaches information that already traveled through the window in the previous layer, so the theoretical receptive field grows with the number of layers stacked.

questions.prompt: What's a key pitfall of pure sliding window attention?
options: It cannot be implemented on modern GPUs
It struggles with tasks needing precise long-range retrieval unless paired with global or hybrid layers
It always uses more memory than full attention
It only works with recurrent architectures, not transformers
questions.explanation: Because a single layer can't directly connect tokens farther apart than the window, tasks that need one precise long-distance link (like needle-in-a-haystack retrieval) can fail without enough depth or hybrid global-attention layers.

posts.title: BDH-CQ: A 150M Model That Reasons Without Words
posts.subtitle: Pathway's brain-inspired network solves ARC-AGI puzzles by iterating in latent space instead of writing chain-of-thought tokens
posts.summary: Pathway's BDH-CQ reasons by continuously updating a recurrent latent memory instead of generating chain-of-thought text, and at 150M parameters it broke the ARC-AGI-1 cost-accuracy frontier: about 11x cheaper per task than GPT-5.6 Luna (Low), though still 4.7 points behind on raw accuracy.

slides.title: A Model That Thinks Without Ever Writing a Word
slides.body: 150 million parameters. No chain-of-thought. It still cracks ARC-AGI-1 puzzles for a fraction of a cent each.
bullets: 29.5% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1
$0.0007 per task in compute
Built on the brain-inspired 'Dragon Hatchling' architecture

slides.title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Is Paid For By the Token
slides.body: Most reasoning models 'think out loud': every intermediate step is a generated token, and every generated token is billed.
bullets: GPT-5.6 Luna at low reasoning effort costs about $0.040 per ARC-AGI-1 task
Longer reasoning traces mean higher latency and cost, not just better answers
The reasoning itself is never stored anywhere except as generated text

slides.title: Dragon Hatchling: Reasoning as a Recurrent Latent State
slides.body: BDH-CQ is built on BDH ('Baby Dragon Hatchling'), a post-transformer architecture inspired by local, Hebbian-like neuron interactions instead of pure attention over a growing cache.
bullets: Inputs at inference time continuously update a recurrent associative memory
The model iterates on that latent state to solve a query — no text is generated as scratch work
A sequence of in-context examples gets compressed into a fixed-size memory representation, not a growing KV cache

slides.title: Cheaper, Not Better — a Real Tradeoff
slides.body: Pathway's claim is precise: BDH-CQ breaks the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier, not the accuracy record.
bullets: Numbers are from Pathway's public ARC-AGI-1 evaluation, September 2026

slides.title: Solving a Puzzle Without Narrating It
slides.body: Picture an ARC-AGI grid task: a handful of example input/output grid pairs, then a new input grid to complete.
bullets: BDH-CQ reads the example pairs and folds their pattern into its recurrent latent memory as it goes
For the new query grid, it iterates internally in that latent space — refining a hidden representation of 'the rule'
It emits only the final answer grid; there is no intermediate 'first I notice X, then Y' text to inspect

slides.title: Where This Breaks Down
slides.body: Cheap and clever isn't the same as ready to replace chain-of-thought everywhere.
bullets: It's still 4.7 accuracy points behind Luna on the same benchmark — the frontier is about efficiency, not superiority
No text reasoning trace means no easy way to audit *why* it answered as it did — a real cost for debugging or safety review
Proven so far only at 150M parameters on ARC-AGI-1; scaling experiments (1B–600B) show promising trends but aren't yet a finished product

slides.title: Why It's Worth Watching
slides.body: BDH-CQ doesn't kill chain-of-thought reasoning, but it's real evidence that verbalizing every reasoning step isn't the only path to solving reasoning tasks.
bullets: A genuinely different reasoning mechanism — recurrent latent iteration — not just a bigger or better-tuned transformer
If it scales past 150M while keeping its cost advantage, it changes the economics of cheap, high-volume reasoning workloads
Interpretability and the accuracy gap are the two things to watch before it's production-ready

questions.prompt: What does BDH-CQ do differently from typical chain-of-thought reasoning models?
options: It uses a much larger KV cache than usual
It reasons through iterative computation in a recurrent latent space without generating intermediate text tokens
It requires human-written reasoning traces at inference time
It only works through a paid API with no open weights
questions.explanation: BDH-CQ continuously updates a recurrent latent memory and iterates on it internally — it never writes out a chain-of-thought, which is exactly what makes it cheap.

Higher accuracy and higher cost
Lower accuracy and higher cost
questions.explanation: BDH-CQ scores 29.5% vs Luna's 34.2% pass@2, but costs about $0.0007 per task versus Luna's ~$0.040 — roughly 11x cheaper, with a real accuracy gap, not a free win.

questions.prompt: What underlies the 'Dragon Hatchling' (BDH) architecture's design?
options: A standard multi-head transformer with a larger context window
Brain-inspired local, Hebbian-like interactions with sparse, persistent activation state
A retrieval-augmented lookup table over a document index
Diffusion-based denoising of the output tokens
questions.explanation: BDH draws on neuroscience principles — local interaction, sparse activity, and a persistent state that updates continually — rather than attention over an ever-growing cache.

slides.title: 9 Billion DNA Variants, Every Effect Pre-Scored
slides.body: Instead of running a model on demand for every DNA variant a researcher cares about, DeepMind just scored all of them in advance.
bullets: ~9 billion single-nucleotide variants covered
1 petabyte of precomputed predictions
Free browser access for research use

slides.title: On-Demand Variant Scoring Doesn't Scale
slides.body: AlphaGenome, DeepMind's sequence model, predicts how a DNA change affects gene expression, splicing, and chromatin from a 1-megabase window of context — but running it fresh for every variant a study needs is slow and compute-heavy.
bullets: Rare-disease and GWAS follow-up studies often need scores for thousands to millions of candidate variants at once
Each on-demand query means re-running a large model over a long DNA window
That cost discourages exploring variants outside a study's original hypothesis

slides.title: Precompute Everything, Then Just Look It Up
slides.body: The Atlas runs AlphaGenome across every genome position and every possible substitution, then serves the results as a lookup rather than a live inference call.
bullets: A large teacher ensemble's predictions are distilled into a faster student model, completing all-modality predictions for one variant in under a second on an H100
Results for all ~3 billion positions × 3 possible substitutions (~9B variants) are stored at 1 petabyte scale — over 30x the size of the AlphaFold Database
A new AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score merges AlphaGenome's regulatory predictions with AlphaMissense's protein-coding predictions into one number per variant

slides.title: How Big Is 1 Petabyte of Genome Predictions?
bullets: Scale comparison to DeepMind's earlier structural-biology resource

slides.title: What It Found in the UK Biobank

The signal came from variants outside protein-coding genes — exactly where per-query scoring is least likely to be run by default

slides.title: What the Atlas Isn't
slides.body: A precomputed score is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis.
bullets: Predictions are computational estimates, not experimentally validated for every one of the 9 billion variants
The fast student model trades some accuracy for speed versus running the full teacher ensemble directly
Free access today is for non-commercial/academic use; commercial availability via Google Cloud is described as coming later, so it isn't yet a drop-in for clinical production pipelines

slides.body: The Atlas shifts genomics workflows from 'run the model per query' to 'look up a precomputed atlas' — the same pattern that made AlphaFold Database transformative for structural biology.
bullets: Biggest impact is likely in non-coding regions, historically the hardest to interpret and the least queried
Watch for commercial/clinical availability and independent validation of specific high-impact predictions
The AVI score gives researchers one number to triage millions of candidate variants before deeper follow-up

posts.title: GQA: The Memory Trick Behind Fast LLM Serving
posts.subtitle: Why Llama 3 and Mistral share key/value heads across groups of query heads instead of giving every head its own
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention shares one key/value head across a cluster of query heads instead of giving every head its own, shrinking the KV cache and speeding up serving with only a small quality cost — which is why it's the default in Llama 2/3, Mistral, and most modern open LLMs.

slides.title: One KV Cache, Shared By Many Query Heads
slides.body: Most modern open LLMs don't give every attention head its own key/value pair anymore — they share.
bullets: Used in Llama 2, Llama 3, Mistral, and most modern open-weight LLMs
Sits between two older extremes: full multi-head and single shared-head attention

slides.title: The KV Cache Is What Makes Serving Expensive
slides.body: In standard multi-head attention (MHA), each of H attention heads keeps its own key (K) and value (V) vectors for every token generated so far.
bullets: KV cache size scales with number of heads × sequence length × batch size — not with model weight size
That cache, not the model weights, is often what limits how many concurrent requests a GPU can actually serve
Longer conversations and bigger batches make the problem worse, not better

slides.title: Multi-Query, Then Grouped-Query
slides.body: Multi-Query Attention (MQA) tried the extreme fix: one shared KV head for every query head — big memory savings, but a noticeable quality drop. GQA (Ainslie et al., Google, 2023) is the tunable middle ground.
bullets: Query heads are split into G groups; every head in a group shares one KV head, where 1 < G < H
Existing MHA checkpoints can be converted via 'uptraining' — mean-pooling grouped heads' K/V projections, then continuing pretraining on roughly 5% of the original compute
G is a dial: G close to H behaves like MHA, G close to 1 behaves like MQA

slides.title: Three Points on the Same Dial
bullets: H = total attention heads, G = number of shared KV groups

slides.title: Llama 2 70B's 8:1 Ratio
slides.body: Llama 2 70B uses 64 query heads but only 8 KV heads — an 8:1 grouping ratio instead of 64 separate KV heads.
bullets: KV cache memory scales with the number of KV heads, so 8 heads instead of 64 cuts that memory roughly 8x at the same sequence length and batch size
Mistral 7B pairs a similar GQA setup (32 query heads, 8 KV heads) with sliding-window attention for extra memory savings
That freed-up memory is what lets a server pack more concurrent sequences onto the same GPU

slides.title: Where the Dial Can Go Wrong
slides.body: GQA isn't a free lunch — it's a tradeoff you're choosing a point on.
bullets: Push G too low and you reprise MQA's quality loss, especially on tasks needing fine per-head specialization
The right group count is workload- and model-specific, and typically found empirically rather than by formula
Converting a pretrained MHA model to GQA needs the uptraining step — you can't just drop KV heads at inference time without retraining

slides.title: Check the Ratio, Not Just the Params
slides.body: GQA is now the default choice for serving-oriented open LLMs because it keeps most of MHA's quality at a fraction of MQA's memory footprint.
bullets: A model card's `num_key_value_heads` vs `num_attention_heads` tells you exactly where it sits on the MHA–MQA dial
Fewer KV heads means more concurrent requests per GPU, all else equal
It's an inference-serving optimization, not a training-time accuracy trick

questions.prompt: What problem does Grouped-Query Attention primarily address?
options: Slow tokenizer throughput on long documents
The KV cache's memory footprint during inference
Poor quality of training data
Limits on positional encoding range
questions.explanation: The KV cache — not the model's weights — is often the binding constraint on how many requests a GPU can serve at once. GQA shrinks it by sharing KV heads across groups of query heads.

questions.prompt: How does GQA relate to Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA)?
options: It's identical to MQA
It's a tunable middle ground — grouping query heads to share a smaller number of KV heads, between MHA's one-per-head and MQA's single shared head
It adds more KV heads than MHA uses
It removes the attention mechanism entirely
questions.explanation: GQA groups query heads into clusters that each share one KV head — a dial you can set anywhere between MHA (one KV head per query head, G=H) and MQA (a single shared KV head, G=1).

questions.prompt: In Llama 2 70B, using 8 KV heads instead of 64 does what to KV cache memory, holding sequence length and batch size fixed?
options: Increases it roughly 8x
Roughly cuts it 8x
Has no effect on memory, only on output quality
Eliminates the KV cache entirely
questions.explanation: KV cache size scales with the number of KV heads, so going from 64 separate heads to 8 shared groups cuts that memory roughly 8x, letting more sequences fit in the same GPU memory.

posts.title: Miles v0.1: Decoupling RL Rollout From Training
posts.subtitle: Why the fastest RL post-training loop is the one that never waits
posts.summary: Miles v0.1, from RadixArk (the SGLang team's spinoff, built on Tsinghua's slime), redesigns the LLM RL post-training loop so rollout generation and training run fully asynchronously instead of lockstep, reporting 3x rollout throughput, 10x faster weight sync, and 30x faster weight conversion.

slides.title: The RL Loop Has Three Stages. Most Frameworks Run Them in Lockstep.
slides.body: Generate rollouts, train on them, sync the updated weights back to the rollout engines. Miles v0.1 asks: what if none of these had to wait for the others?

slides.title: Rollout Generation Dominates Wall-Clock Time — and Idles the Trainer
slides.body: In a synchronous RL loop, the trainer GPUs sit idle while the rollout engine generates trajectories, and the rollout engines sit idle while the trainer updates weights. Since rollout generation is the slowest stage, that idle time compounds every step.
bullets: Lockstep scheduling: generate → train → sync, one stage at a time
Whichever stage is slowest sets the pace for both sets of GPUs
At frontier scale (MoE models, long trajectories), that waste is expensive hardware sitting idle

slides.title: Fully Asynchronous RL: Generate and Train Concurrently
slides.body: Miles decouples rollout (built on SGLang) from training (Megatron-LM or PyTorch FSDP), orchestrated over Ray. In async mode, rollout engines keep generating trajectories continuously; the trainer consumes whichever trajectories are finished whenever it needs its next batch.
bullets: Rollout engine: SGLang — keeps producing trajectories nonstop
Trainer: Megatron-LM or FSDP — pulls a batch whenever it's ready, no waiting
Three weight-sync transports, chosen per deployment topology (colocated vs. disaggregated GPU pools)

slides.title: The Reported Gains: 3x, 10x, 30x
slides.body: Compared to the earlier lockstep design, RadixArk reports large, stage-specific speedups — the biggest gain is in weight conversion, the mechanical step of reshaping trained weights back into a format the rollout engine can load.

slides.title: Worked Example: Training a MoE Model With GRPO
slides.body: Say you're running GRPO post-training on a large mixture-of-experts model. In the old lockstep design, the trainer finishes a step and then waits ~30-60s while weights get converted and pushed to every rollout worker before generation can resume.
bullets: Async mode: rollout workers keep generating on the previous policy version while conversion happens in the background
The trainer immediately starts consuming newly-finished trajectories for its next batch — no dead time
Miles supports GRPO, GSPO, PPO, REINFORCE++, plus SFT and on-policy distillation, on the same stack

slides.title: The Tradeoff: Staleness
slides.body: Async throughput isn't free. A rollout generated while the trainer was mid-update was sampled from a slightly older policy than the one it's eventually trained against — a staleness gap that grows if training falls behind generation.
bullets: More staleness = faster throughput but a noisier training signal
Not worth the added system complexity for small-scale, single-GPU fine-tuning jobs
Runs on NVIDIA GB300/GB200/B300/B200/H200/H100/A100 and AMD MI300X/MI325/MI350/MI355X via ROCm — but tuning the async schedule per cluster is nontrivial

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: The RL post-training loop has 3 stages: rollout, train, sync weights — Miles's core idea is decoupling them instead of running them in lockstep
SGLang handles rollout, Megatron-LM/FSDP handles training, Ray orchestrates — with 3 weight-sync transports for different cluster topologies
Reported gains: 3x rollout throughput, 10x weight sync, 30x weight conversion vs. the earlier synchronous design
The cost of async is policy staleness — a real tradeoff, not a free lunch
Miles descends from THUDM's slime, built jointly by RadixArk (the SGLang team's spinout), InfiXAI, and Ant Group's RL teams

questions.prompt: In a synchronous (lockstep) RL post-training loop, why do trainer GPUs sit idle?
options: They're waiting for the rollout engine to finish generating trajectories before training can start
They run out of memory during rollout generation
Megatron-LM requires a manual restart between steps
SGLang blocks all GPU access during inference
questions.explanation: Lockstep scheduling means generate → train → sync happen one at a time; whichever stage is slowest (usually rollout generation) leaves the other stage's hardware idle while it waits.

questions.prompt: What is the main tradeoff Miles's fully asynchronous mode introduces?
options: Higher GPU memory usage across the board
Policy staleness — some rollouts are sampled from a slightly older policy version
Loss of support for GRPO and PPO
Inability to run on AMD hardware
questions.explanation: Because rollout generation and training run concurrently, some trajectories are generated from a policy snapshot that's already been updated by the time training uses them — a staleness gap that trades signal freshness for throughput.

questions.prompt: Which reported improvement was the largest in Miles v0.1?
options: Rollout throughput (3x)
Weight synchronization (10x)
Weight conversion (30x)
Model accuracy (2x)
questions.explanation: RadixArk reports weight conversion — reshaping trained weights into a format the rollout engine can load — improved 30x, the largest of the three reported gains.
