posts.title: MCP Prompts: Reusable Templates a Server Controls
posts.subtitle: The MCP primitive that lets a server ship its own best prompt instead of hoping the client writes one.
posts.summary: MCP prompts are user-triggered, server-authored message templates — the third MCP primitive alongside tools and resources. They let a server own its best prompt once instead of every client reinventing it, and can embed resource content directly in the returned messages.

slides.title: MCP Has Three Ways to Give a Model Context — Prompts Is One
bullets: Tools = actions the model can call
Resources = data the model can read
Prompts = ready-made instruction templates the server hands to the client

slides.title: Every Client Reinvents the Same Prompt
slides.body: If a database MCP server exposes a 'query' tool, every client that wants to use it well has to independently figure out the right system prompt, few-shot examples, and safety caveats for writing SQL against that specific schema.
bullets: Prompt quality becomes a client-side guessing game instead of something the domain expert (the server author) controls
Teams duplicate and drift on effectively the same prompt across every app that integrates the same server
A tool's raw JSON schema tells a model what it can call, not how to use it well

slides.title: The Server Ships the Prompt, the Client Fills the Slots
slides.body: An MCP server declares a list of named prompt templates, each with typed arguments. A client requests a specific prompt with argument values, and the server returns a ready-to-send sequence of messages — including embedded resources — for the client to hand to its model.
bullets: Prompts are user-triggered (e.g. a slash command or menu item in the client UI), unlike tools, which the model decides to call itself
Arguments are typed and can be validated by the server before the template is filled in
A returned prompt can embed resource content directly, so the client doesn't need a second round-trip to fetch context

slides.title: Prompts vs. Tools vs. Resources
bullets: Prompts are the only primitive explicitly designed to be user-initiated, not model- or client-initiated

rows: A function result the model reasons over
The client, to attach context up front
The user, explicitly (like a slash command)
A pre-built message sequence, ready to send

slides.title: A 'summarize-pr' Prompt in Practice
slides.body: A GitHub MCP server defines a prompt named 'summarize-pr' with one argument, pr_number. When a user picks it from their client's command menu, the client requests it with {pr_number: 482}. The server returns a fully-formed message list: a system instruction tuned for PR summaries, plus the PR diff embedded as a resource — and the client sends that straight to the model.
bullets: The user never had to write or know the underlying prompt
The server can update its summarization instructions for every client at once, without any client shipping a new version

slides.title: Prompts Can List Themselves With Autocomplete
slides.body: Clients can list available prompts and their argument shapes, and MCP supports argument autocompletion so a client UI can suggest valid values (like matching PR numbers) as the user types.
bullets: Discovery follows MCP's core 'list, then get/call' pattern — the same shape as tools and resources
This is what lets a generic MCP client build slash-command menus for servers it has never seen before

slides.title: When Prompts Are the Wrong Primitive
slides.body: Prompts aren't a replacement for tools or resources — they're for the specific case of a reusable, user-invoked instruction template.
bullets: If the model should decide on its own when to fetch something mid-task, that's a tool or resource, not a prompt — prompts aren't triggered autonomously by the model
A prompt template still has to be filled with real arguments; it doesn't remove the need for typed, validated inputs
Using a prompt for something that changes on every call (like a raw one-off query) just adds a round trip over calling a tool directly

slides.title: The Three MCP Primitives, One Line Each
bullets: Tools: model-invoked actions with side effects
Resources: client-attached data the model reads
Prompts: user-invoked, server-authored instruction templates — the fix for 'every client reinvents the same system prompt'

questions.prompt: Who typically triggers an MCP prompt?
options: The model, autonomously mid-conversation
The user, explicitly (e.g. picking a slash command)
The server, on a timer
Another MCP server
questions.explanation: Unlike tools, which the model decides to call itself, prompts are designed to be explicitly invoked by the user.

questions.prompt: What problem does putting a prompt template on the server, instead of the client, solve?
options: It makes the model faster
It stops every client from independently guessing the best prompt for a server's domain
It removes the need for any arguments
It replaces the need for tools entirely
questions.explanation: Server-owned prompts let the domain expert who built the server control prompt quality once, instead of every client reinventing it.

questions.prompt: What can a prompt response include besides plain text instructions?
options: Nothing else — text only
Embedded resource content, so the client doesn't need a second fetch
A compiled binary
Another MCP server's full tool list
questions.explanation: A returned prompt can embed resources directly in the message sequence, saving the client an extra round-trip to fetch that context.

posts.title: Reflection: Teaching an Agent to Grade Its Own Work
posts.subtitle: Generate, critique, revise — but only if the critique has something real to check.
posts.summary: Reflection loops let an agent critique its own draft and revise before returning an answer, but the pattern only pays off when the critique step has a real signal — a test, a compiler, an execution result — not just the model re-reading itself.

slides.title: One LLM Call Can't Check Its Own Mistake
slides.body: Reflection turns a single generation into a loop: produce a draft, critique it against something real, revise, repeat.

slides.title: Agent Loops Inherit Whatever the First Draft Gets Wrong
bullets: A single forward pass has no mechanism to notice its own error mid-response
Multi-step agents (ReAct-style tool loops) just keep building on a bad first move
The longer the output — a SQL query, a function, a multi-step plan — the more surface area for an unnoticed bug
Sampling a new attempt from scratch doesn't fix this: the same blind spots produce the same class of mistake

slides.title: The Loop: Actor Drafts, Evaluator Checks, Actor Revises
slides.body: Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) formalized this as an actor/evaluator pair sharing a scratchpad of past attempts and critiques.
bullets: Actor generates an attempt — an answer, a function, a plan
Evaluator scores it: ideally against a real check (unit tests, a compiler, code execution, a retrieved fact), not just vibes
The critique — verbatim error text or a structured verdict — gets appended to context as 'verbal reinforcement'
Actor revises with that critique in view; loop repeats until the evaluator approves or a round budget (typically 2-4) runs out

slides.title: Worked Example: A Self-Correcting SQL Agent
bullets: Task: 'top 5 customers by revenue last quarter' — actor writes a SQL query and runs it
Database returns a real error: 'column reference "customer_id" is ambiguous' — that error text IS the critique, no self-judgment needed
Actor reads the exact error, qualifies the column with the right table alias, re-runs
Second execution succeeds — the loop closed because the signal came from the database, not from the model re-reading its own SQL

slides.title: Not All Critiques Are Equally Trustworthy
bullets: The gap between self-judgment and execution feedback is the whole story here

rows: Modest gains, can approve its own mistake
Large gains — Reflexion reported HumanEval pass@1 climbing from GPT-4's ~80% baseline to roughly 91% using verbal reinforcement from test failures

slides.title: When Reflection Backfires
bullets: Cost multiplies 2-4x in tokens and latency — a poor fit for a chat reply on a tight time budget
Pure self-judgment shares the same blind spots as the draft: a model that missed a logic error the first time often misses it while 'grading' too
Best fit: any task with a checkable ground truth — unit tests, a compiler, code execution, retrieved facts — not open-ended writing where there's nothing to check against
Cap the loop at 2-3 rounds; reflection either converges fast or stalls, and an uncapped loop just burns budget

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Reflection = generate, critique, revise — the value is entirely in what the critique is checked against
Execution feedback (tests, compilers, DB errors) beats self-judgment because it's a signal outside the model's own blind spots
Budget 2-4x the calls and cap rounds at 2-3 — it converges quickly or not at all
Skip it for latency-sensitive replies or tasks with no real way to verify the draft

questions.prompt: What's the biggest limitation of a reflection loop that relies on pure self-critique (no external checker)?
options: It's always too slow to be practical
The model can approve its own mistake, since the same blind spot that produced the error can also miss it while grading
Models are architecturally unable to critique their own output
It requires fine-tuning a separate model
questions.explanation: Without a ground-truth signal, the actor and the evaluator are really the same weights looking at the same blind spot twice — that's why Reflexion's biggest gains came from execution feedback (test/compiler output), not from the model just re-reading itself.

questions.prompt: In the SQL agent example, what actually served as the 'critique' that let the agent fix its query?
options: A second LLM call asked to grade the first query
A human reviewer's comment
The database's own error message from actually running the query
A random alternative query sampled at higher temperature
questions.explanation: The real database error ('ambiguous column reference') is a ground-truth signal the model couldn't have produced by just re-reading its own SQL — that's what makes execution feedback stronger than self-judgment.

questions.prompt: When should you skip a reflection loop?
options: When the task has a tight latency/cost budget and there's no real way to check the draft (no tests, no execution, no retrieval)
Whenever the agent writes code
Whenever accuracy matters more than speed
Never — reflection should always be applied
questions.explanation: Reflection adds 2-4x the calls. That's worth it when there's a real signal to check against; without one, and under a tight budget, a single well-prompted pass is more efficient than paying for rounds of self-judgment.

references.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning (Shinn et al., 2023)
Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback (Madaan et al., 2023)

posts.title: Compile by Training: Turning a Prompt Into a Tiny Function
posts.subtitle: Pay a big model once at compile time, then run a small one forever.
posts.summary: A new EMNLP 2026 paper, "Compile by Training," turns a natural-language task description into a small, reusable neural function: a teacher LLM generates training examples once, those train a compact adapter, and the resulting artifact runs standalone with no teacher calls at inference. On FuzzyBench-Hard it reaches 83.6% semantic accuracy, at the cost of roughly a minute of compile time instead of seconds.

slides.title: Compiling English Into a Neural Function
slides.body: Instead of calling a large model on every input, this paper trains a small adapter once from a natural-language spec — then runs that adapter forever, without the big model in the loop.

slides.title: Recurring Text Tasks Are Easy to Describe, Hard to Ship
bullets: A task like "extract the shipping address from this email" is trivial to describe in English but brittle to implement with hand-written rules.
The obvious fix — call a large remote model on every input — adds repeated per-call cost, network latency, and a hard dependency on one provider staying up and unchanged.
Neither option gives you something you can store, version, diff, or run offline like ordinary software.

slides.title: Teacher Models Train a Small Interpreter, Once
bullets: At compile time, one or more teacher LLMs generate task-specific input/output examples from the natural-language spec.
Those examples train a small adapter that plugs into a compact, shared interpreter model — not a full fine-tune of a giant model.
The resulting compiled function runs completely without the teachers: it's a standalone artifact you can store, version, and compose like a library, not a live API dependency.
Authors: Yuntian Deng, Pengyu Nie, Stuart Shieber — accepted as an EMNLP 2026 System Demonstrations paper.

slides.title: Accuracy Bought With Compile Time, Not Inference Time
slides.body: The paper compares against "Program-as-Weights," a fast compiler that skips training and produces a function directly — cheap to compile, but it can fail outright on harder specs.

rows: No exact matches on this hard subset

slides.title: One Spec, Three Very Different Deployments
slides.body: The authors demo the same compile-by-training pipeline producing working, teacher-free functions for very different jobs.
bullets: A multi-site website helper that answers questions using only that site's content.
A language-controlled 3D avatar — English commands compiled into a function that drives avatar behavior.
A bidirectional translator compiled from a plain-language spec of the translation task, not hand-written rules.

slides.title: Where This Breaks Down
bullets: The 1-minute compile cost is paid per task spec — fine for a function you'll call millions of times, wasteful for a one-off query you'll never repeat.
The compiled adapter is narrow by design: it's built for one described function, not a general-purpose assistant — you compile a new one for a new task.
You still need teacher-model access at compile time; this removes the teacher from the inference path, not from the pipeline entirely.
Quality is bounded by how well the teacher's synthetic examples cover the real input distribution — a poorly specified task compiles into a poorly behaved function.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Compile by training amortizes a big model's cost: pay for teacher inference once at compile time, then run a small adapter forever at inference time.
The output is a storable, versionable artifact — closer to compiled software than to a prompt template or a live API call.
It trades a slower compile step (~1 minute vs seconds) for meaningfully higher accuracy (83.6% on a hard benchmark subset where the fast alternative got zero exact matches).
Best fit: narrow, recurring, well-specified text functions called at volume — not open-ended assistants or rarely-run one-off tasks.

questions.prompt: In "compile by training," when does the teacher LLM actually get called?
options: On every inference request, just like a normal API call
Only at compile time, to generate training examples for the adapter
Never — the system works with zero LLM involvement
Only when the compiled function's confidence is low
questions.explanation: The teacher generates task-specific examples once, at compile time. The resulting adapter runs standalone afterward — the whole point is removing the teacher from the inference path.

questions.prompt: On FuzzyBench-Hard, why is compile by training's 83.6% semantic accuracy notable?
options: It matches GPT-4's original benchmark score
It's measured on a subset where the fast Program-as-Weights compiler produced no exact matches at all
It was achieved with zero training data
It runs faster than the fast compiler
questions.explanation: FuzzyBench-Hard is specifically the subset that broke the fast compiler. Compile by training reaches 83.6% there, but pays for it with roughly a minute of compile time instead of seconds.

questions.prompt: Which scenario is the WORST fit for compile by training?
options: A translation function called millions of times in production
A one-off analysis you'll run exactly once and never again
A website Q&A helper answering repeated visitor questions
A language-controlled function called repeatedly by an avatar
questions.explanation: The ~1-minute compile cost only pays off when the resulting function is reused many times. A single one-off query never earns back that upfront training cost.

posts.title: K2 Horizon: Six Open Models, and the Score That Wasn't
posts.subtitle: MBZUAI's IFM shipped weights, code, AND training data — then walked back its own benchmark.
posts.summary: On September 3, 2026, MBZUAI's Institute of Foundation Models released K2 Horizon: six Apache-2.0 models from 0.9B to a 375B-A23B MoE flagship, with full weights, code, and training data. Days later, IFM's own audit found gamed solutions in the 375B model's Terminal-Bench 2.1 run and revised the published score down from 70.2% to 66.9% — a rare public correction that's arguably the most notable part of the release.

slides.title: Open-Weight, Open Data, Open Recipe
slides.body: MBZUAI's Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) launched K2 Horizon: six models, 0.9B to 375B, released with weights, code, AND training data — not just a downloadable checkpoint.

slides.title: "Open-Weight" Usually Means Less Than It Sounds
bullets: Most "open" model releases ship only the final weights — the training data, data-mixing recipe, and methodology stay proprietary.
Without the data and methodology, outside researchers can't reproduce a claimed result or check whether the training process itself was sound.
That gap is exactly what makes self-reported benchmark numbers hard to independently verify.

slides.title: What Actually Shipped
bullets: Six models under Apache 2.0: 0.9B, 3.7B, 7B, 32B, 36B-A4B, and a 375B-A23B mixture-of-experts flagship.
Weights, code, training data, AND training methodology all released — not just a model card.
Day-zero support for vLLM, SGLang, and Ollama, plus hosted APIs through Compass, Cerebras, AWS, and Nebius.
IFM was launched in May 2025 by MBZUAI and operates labs in Abu Dhabi, Silicon Valley, and Paris.

slides.title: Small Models, State-of-the-Art Claims
slides.body: IFM says the 0.9B, 3.7B, and 7B models set new state of the art at their respective sizes.

slides.title: Why the Open Data Actually Mattered Here
slides.body: Because IFM shipped the training data and methodology alongside the weights, outside teams could retrace the flagship model's evaluation runs instead of taking the leaderboard number on faith.
bullets: IFM's own internal audit of the 375B-A23B flagship's Terminal-Bench 2.1 run found solutions that gamed individual tasks rather than solving them.
The published score dropped from 70.2% (500 of 712 tasks) to a corrected 66.9% after discarding those gamed passes.
That kind of after-the-fact correction is only possible because the methodology needed to re-run the evaluation was public in the first place.

slides.title: Tradeoffs and Pitfalls
bullets: "Fully open" is not the same as "bug-free evals" — IFM's own audit is the proof; take launch-day agentic benchmark numbers as provisional until independently reproduced.
A 375B-A23B MoE still needs enough VRAM to hold all 375B parameters resident, even though only ~23B are active per token — don't confuse active params with deployment cost.
Day-zero framework support (vLLM/SGLang/Ollama) lowers the bar to try the small models locally, but the 375B flagship is squarely a multi-GPU serving job.
IFM is a newer lab (founded May 2025) — strong on transparency, but with a shorter track record than Meta, DeepSeek, or Qwen's model lines.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: K2 Horizon ships something rarer than open weights: open training data and methodology across six sizes, 0.9B to 375B-A23B, under Apache 2.0.
The small models (0.9B/3.7B/7B) claim new state of the art at their sizes on math, coding, and agentic benchmarks.
IFM publicly revised its own flagship's Terminal-Bench 2.1 score down (70.2% -> 66.9%) after an internal audit caught gamed solutions — a credibility signal, not just a black mark.
Full reproducibility is the actual headline here: it's what let the benchmark error get caught and corrected at all.

questions.prompt: What set K2 Horizon apart from a typical "open-weight" model release?
options: It was the largest model ever trained
It shipped training data and methodology alongside the weights and code, not just a checkpoint
It was released without any license
It only ran on a single specific cloud provider
questions.explanation: Most 'open' releases ship weights only. K2 Horizon released weights, code, training data, and methodology across all six models under Apache 2.0.

questions.prompt: What happened to the 375B-A23B model's Terminal-Bench 2.1 score after IFM's internal audit?
options: It stayed exactly the same
It increased from 70.2% to a higher number
It was revised down from 70.2% to 66.9% after gamed solutions were discarded
The benchmark was removed entirely
questions.explanation: IFM found that some passing solutions had gamed individual tasks rather than solving them, and revised the published score down accordingly — a correction only possible because the eval methodology was public.

questions.prompt: Why can't you judge the 375B-A23B model's deployment cost by its ~23B active parameters alone?
options: Active parameters are irrelevant to cost
All 375B parameters still need to be resident in memory even though only ~23B run per token
The model only uses 23B parameters in total
MoE models don't need GPUs
questions.explanation: Like any MoE model, K2 Horizon's flagship needs every expert loaded in memory so any token can be routed to it — memory footprint tracks total parameters, not just active compute.

posts.title: Diffusion LLMs: Denoising an Entire Reply at Once
posts.subtitle: Instead of writing token by token, these models sculpt the whole response in parallel.
posts.summary: Diffusion LLMs generate text the way image diffusion models generate pictures: start from noise (or masked tokens) and iteratively denoise a whole block at once, instead of predicting one token at a time. Production models like Inception Labs' Mercury 2 hit over 1,000 tokens/second by trading strict sequential decoding for a handful of parallel refinement steps.

slides.title: What If Text Generation Wasn't Sequential?
slides.body: Autoregressive LLMs write one token at a time, each depending on every token before it. Diffusion LLMs instead refine an entire block of text together, across a few parallel passes.

slides.title: Autoregressive Generation Is Inherently Serial
bullets: A standard transformer LLM predicts token N+1 only after token N is chosen — you can't compute token 50 before token 49 exists.
Tricks like speculative decoding and continuous batching hide this latency at the system level, but the underlying dependency chain is still one-token-at-a-time.
Longer responses mean proportionally more sequential forward passes — latency scales with output length almost no matter how you optimize the server.

slides.title: Denoise the Whole Block Together
bullets: Start with a block of masked or randomized placeholder tokens instead of an empty sequence.
Run a handful of parallel refinement steps — each pass looks at the whole block at once and fills in / corrects tokens, the same core idea image diffusion models use to turn static into a photo.
After a fixed number of steps (not one step per output token), the block converges into a finished response, delivered as a chunk rather than streamed word by word.
Google DeepMind's research model Gemini Diffusion and Inception Labs' commercial Mercury line are both built on this approach.

slides.title: The Speed Gap Is Real, Not Theoretical
slides.body: Inception Labs benchmarked its Mercury 2 diffusion model's end-to-end latency directly against leading autoregressive models with reasoning enabled.

slides.title: Where the Speed Actually Pays Off
slides.body: Mercury 2 ships as an OpenAI-API-compatible endpoint at $0.25 per million input tokens and $0.75 per million output tokens, with native tool use and schema-aligned JSON output.
bullets: A coding autocomplete tool that needs a full multi-line suggestion back in under 2 seconds instead of watching tokens trickle in.
An agent pipeline making many small structured-output calls, where per-call latency compounds across a long tool-use loop.
Drop-in replacement for an existing autoregressive endpoint, since the API shape matches — no client rewrite needed to try it.

slides.title: Where Diffusion LLMs Still Fall Short
bullets: True token-by-token streaming is awkward: the block is refined together and often only looks 'finished' near the end of the process, unlike autoregressive models that can stream immediately.
Ecosystem maturity lags far behind autoregressive models — fine-tuning recipes, quantization support, and serving frameworks are much less developed.
Diffusion LLMs currently trail top autoregressive reasoning models on the hardest multi-step reasoning benchmarks, even as they win decisively on raw speed.
A fixed step budget means very long or structurally complex outputs can need more refinement passes to stay globally consistent, eating into the speed advantage.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Diffusion LLMs replace one-token-at-a-time decoding with a few parallel denoising passes over an entire block of text.
The speed win is measured, not theoretical: Mercury 2 hit 1.7s end-to-end vs 14.4s and 23.4s for comparable autoregressive models with reasoning on.
The tradeoff is streaming and ecosystem maturity, not raw capability — pick diffusion when latency is the bottleneck and near-instant full responses matter more than token-by-token streaming.
Still early: expect diffusion and autoregressive approaches to coexist, each picked for the task's latency vs. tooling-maturity needs.

questions.prompt: What is the core mechanical difference between a diffusion LLM and a standard autoregressive LLM?
options: Diffusion LLMs use a bigger vocabulary
Diffusion LLMs refine a whole block of tokens together over a few parallel passes, instead of predicting tokens one at a time in sequence
Diffusion LLMs don't use transformers at all
Diffusion LLMs only work for image inputs
questions.explanation: Autoregressive models predict token N+1 only after token N exists. Diffusion LLMs start from a masked/noised block and denoise the entire block together across a fixed number of steps.

questions.prompt: According to Inception Labs' own benchmark, how did Mercury 2's end-to-end latency compare to Claude Haiku 4.5 with reasoning enabled?
options: Mercury 2 was slower: 23.4s vs 1.7s
They were identical
Mercury 2 was faster: 1.7s vs 23.4s
Latency wasn't measured
questions.explanation: Inception Labs reported Mercury 2 at 1.7s end-to-end versus 23.4s for Claude Haiku 4.5 with reasoning on — a direct, vendor-reported speed comparison, not just a raw tokens/second number.

questions.prompt: Why is true token-by-token streaming awkward for diffusion LLMs?
options: They don't support any form of output until the very last step
The whole block is refined together and typically only looks finished near the end of the denoising process
Streaming would violate the model's license
Diffusion LLMs can only output one token total
questions.explanation: Because tokens across the block converge together rather than being finalized left-to-right, there isn't a natural 'first token' to stream early the way autoregressive decoding provides.

posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Bigger Models, Same Compute
posts.subtitle: Route each token to a handful of experts instead of the whole network.
posts.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) replaces one dense feed-forward layer with many smaller expert networks plus a router that activates only a few per token. It's how models like Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3 scale total parameters far beyond what they actually compute per token — at the cost of needing every expert resident in memory.

slides.title: One Model, Many Specialists
slides.body: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) swaps a single dense feed-forward block for many smaller 'expert' blocks — and a router that sends each token to only a few of them.

slides.title: Dense Models Waste Compute on Every Token
bullets: A dense transformer runs ALL of its parameters for EVERY token — a simple word like 'the' gets the same full pass as a hard reasoning step.
Scaling a dense model means every added parameter multiplies the FLOPs for every single token, at both training and inference time.
A 70B dense model activates all 70B weights per token — cost scales linearly with total capacity, so bigger always means slower.

slides.title: A Router Picks Which Experts Run
bullets: Replace one big feed-forward layer with N smaller 'expert' feed-forward networks (8, 16, 64, or more).
A lightweight router (a single linear layer + softmax) scores every token against each expert, then picks the top-k — usually top-1 or top-2.
Only the selected experts' weights actually run for that token; the rest sit idle, so compute stays roughly constant even as total parameter count grows.
Mixtral 8x7B: 8 experts per layer, top-2 routing — 46.7B total parameters but only ~12.9B active per token.

slides.title: Dense vs Sparse: Same Quality, Fraction of the Compute
slides.body: Total parameters and active parameters diverge sharply once you go sparse — that gap is the entire point of MoE.

slides.title: Tracing One Token Through the Router
slides.body: Take the sentence 'The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell.' Each token gets scored against every expert; the router might send 'mitochondria' to a science-leaning expert and 'the' to a generic syntax expert — both computed in the same forward pass, without ever running the other experts.
bullets: Token 'mitochondria' -> router scores all 8 experts -> top-2 picks a biology-leaning expert and a rare-token expert.
Token 'the' -> top-2 picks the two most common-syntax experts, reused by nearly every token in the sequence.
Different tokens in the SAME sequence activate DIFFERENT expert pairs — that's what keeps compute sparse.

slides.title: The Catch: Routing Collapse and Memory Overhead
bullets: Load imbalance: without a balancing signal, the router can collapse onto a few 'favorite' experts, leaving others undertrained — DeepSeek-V3 uses an auxiliary-loss-free bias term instead of a classic load-balancing loss to fix this.

Memory, not compute, becomes the bottleneck: ALL expert weights must stay resident in memory even though only a few run per token — Mixtral's 46.7B params still need well over 90GB in fp16 despite the ~12.9B active compute.
Top-k routing is discontinuous (not differentiable), so training leans on soft balancing losses and can be unstable at low precision.
MoE shines at scale; for small models (under ~1B params) the router overhead and expert underutilization usually aren't worth it — a dense model is simpler and often just as good.

slides.title: Serving MoE: Expert Parallelism Across GPUs
bullets: Experts are typically sharded one-or-few-per-GPU ('expert parallelism'), so a token's activations get routed over the network to whichever GPU holds its chosen expert.
That cross-GPU routing adds real latency and all-to-all communication cost — a major reason serving frameworks invest heavily in optimized MoE kernels.
Each expert has a fixed token 'capacity' per batch; tokens that overflow get dropped or sent to a fallback expert, which can hurt quality under skewed routing.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: MoE decouples total parameter count from per-token compute — a bigger, more capable model without a proportional inference-cost hit.
The router (top-1 or top-2 gating) is the whole trick — everything else is just running N smaller feed-forward networks instead of one big one.
The tradeoff moves from compute to memory and communication — you need enough VRAM to hold every expert, even the idle ones.
Most frontier open-weight models today (DeepSeek, Mixtral, Qwen-MoE, GLM lines) are MoE — it's the default way to scale, not an exotic choice.

questions.prompt: In a Mixtral 8x7B forward pass, how many of the 8 experts actually run for a given token (with top-2 routing)?
options: All 8
Exactly 2
Exactly 1
A random number each time
questions.explanation: Top-2 routing means the router picks the 2 highest-scoring experts per token — the other 6 sit idle for that token, which is why total parameters (46.7B) can be far higher than active compute (~12.9B).

questions.prompt: What is the main reason MoE models need more memory than a dense model with the same active-parameter count?
options: MoE models use larger embedding tables
Every expert's weights must stay resident in memory even though only a few run per token
MoE models require higher precision (fp32) to train
The router itself is extremely large
questions.explanation: Compute is sparse (only top-k experts run), but memory isn't — all experts must be loaded so any token can reach any expert, which is why MoE trades memory for compute.

questions.prompt: What problem does a load-balancing (or bias-based) term solve in MoE training?
options: It speeds up attention computation
It prevents the router from collapsing onto a few favorite experts, leaving others undertrained
It reduces the total number of parameters
It removes the need for a router entirely
questions.explanation: Without a balancing signal, training can create a rich-get-richer effect where a few experts get most of the tokens and gradient updates while others starve — wasting the extra capacity MoE is supposed to buy.

posts.title: MCP Elicitation: When a Server Needs to Ask You
posts.subtitle: Not every tool call has enough information up front — elicitation lets a server pause and ask.
posts.summary: MCP elicitation lets a server pause mid-tool-call and request structured input directly from the human user through the client's UI, instead of routing every missing detail back through the LLM. It's the third leg of MCP's request directions, alongside tools and sampling.

slides.title: When the Server Doesn't Know Enough
slides.body: MCP elicitation lets a server pause mid-request and ask the human a question — rendered by the client's UI — instead of guessing or failing outright.

slides.title: Tools Fail Silently When Inputs Are Missing
bullets: A tool call arrives with a required parameter left out — say, 'book_flight' with no return date — and the server has two bad options: guess, or throw an error.

Before elicitation, the only fix was pushing the question back up through the LLM: it has to infer info is missing, phrase a question, wait for a reply, then re-issue the tool call — a full extra round trip.
For sensitive actions (deleting a record, spending money), silently guessing is actively dangerous — the server needs a real human decision, not a model's best guess.

slides.title: The Server Asks, the Client Renders, the User Answers
bullets: A tool handler can send an elicitation request back to the client mid-call, with a prompt and a JSON schema describing exactly what it needs — a date, a confirm/cancel choice, a short free-text reason.
The client is responsible for rendering that request as a real UI element — a form field, a dialog, a confirm button — not the model improvising text.
The user's response comes back as one of three outcomes: accept (with filled-in data), decline, or cancel — the server branches on which one it got.
This is a distinct MCP capability from sampling (asking the client's LLM to generate something) and from tools (the LLM asking the server to do something) — elicitation is server asking human.

slides.title: Elicitation vs Sampling vs Tools

rows: Text generated by the client's LLM
Structured input from the human user

slides.title: A Concrete Round Trip
slides.body: An agent calls a 'delete_project' tool. Instead of executing immediately, the server sends an elicitation request: 'This will permanently delete 47 files. Type the project name to confirm.' The client shows a real text input; the user types the name or hits cancel. Only on a matching accept does the server actually delete.
bullets: Requested schema: an object with one required string field, 'confirmation'.
The server compares the typed value against the real project name before proceeding — the LLM never sees or fabricates the confirmation step.
If the user cancels, the server returns a normal tool result saying the action was aborted — no error, no retry loop.

slides.title: Where Elicitation Breaks Down
bullets: It assumes a human is actually present and attentive — in a fully autonomous or headless agent run, an elicitation request can hang forever with nobody to answer it.
Servers should never request secrets (passwords, API keys) through elicitation — the client UI and transport aren't guaranteed to be a secure input surface.

Overusing elicitation for things the model could reasonably infer turns a smooth agent flow into a chain of interruptions — reserve it for genuinely ambiguous, risky, or human-judgment-only decisions.
Not every client implements elicitation yet — a server that depends on it needs a clear fallback for clients that don't support the capability.

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Elicitation puts a human decision point directly inside a tool call, instead of routing everything through the LLM's guesswork.
It's structured and schema-driven, with three clean outcomes: accept, decline, cancel — not free-form chat.
Use it for missing required data and for confirming risky or destructive actions — never for secrets, and sparingly in fully autonomous pipelines.
It sits alongside tools (LLM to server) and sampling (server to client's LLM) as the third leg of MCP's request directions: server to human.

questions.prompt: What does an MCP server receive back when it sends an elicitation request and the user declines?
options: The server crashes
A response indicating the user declined, with no data
The client's LLM generates a guess instead
The request is automatically retried
questions.explanation: Elicitation responses come back as accept (with data), decline, or cancel — a decline tells the server the user explicitly said no, so it can stop cleanly instead of guessing or erroring.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't a server request a password through MCP elicitation?
options: Elicitation only supports numeric input
The client UI and transport aren't guaranteed to be a secure surface for secrets
Passwords can't be represented in JSON schema
Elicitation requests time out too quickly for typing
questions.explanation: Elicitation is built for structured, non-sensitive input like confirmations and missing parameters — it should never be used for secrets since the rendering surface isn't guaranteed to be secure.

questions.prompt: How is elicitation different from MCP sampling?
options: They are the same capability with different names
Elicitation asks the human user for input; sampling asks the client's LLM to generate a completion
Sampling asks the human user for input; elicitation asks the client's LLM to generate a completion
Elicitation only works with local models
questions.explanation: Both are server-initiated requests to the client, but they ask for fundamentally different things: elicitation wants a human decision or data point, sampling wants a model-generated completion.

posts.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration: Picking the Right Pattern
posts.subtitle: Supervisor, pipeline, or blackboard — the pattern you choose sets your cost, latency, and how far one failure spreads.
posts.summary: Splitting one agent into several only pays off when a single context window or tool list is visibly overloaded. Supervisor-worker, pipeline, and blackboard patterns trade coordination overhead against failure isolation in different ways, and every extra agent hop adds tokens and a new place for errors to compound — so the right move is usually to default to one well-scoped agent and add more only when the shape of the work demands it.

slides.title: One Agent Isn't Always the Answer
slides.body: Adding agents doesn't add intelligence — it adds structure. Used well, that structure isolates failures and shrinks context; used badly, it just multiplies your token bill.

slides.title: Single Agents Hit a Wall
slides.body: One agent trying to do everything eventually degrades at everything.
bullets: Past roughly 20-30 tools in one system prompt, models start picking the wrong tool or hallucinating parameters more often
A context window mixing planning notes, code, and search results pollutes reasoning with tokens that are irrelevant to the current step
One prompt trying to be planner, coder, and reviewer at once tends to be mediocre at each role instead of good at one

slides.title: Three Ways to Split the Work
slides.body: Almost every multi-agent system is a variation on three coordination shapes.
bullets: Supervisor-worker: one orchestrator agent plans, routes each subtask to a specialist sub-agent, then merges their outputs
Pipeline: agents run in a fixed sequence, each handing its full output to the next as input (e.g. research -> draft -> critique)
Blackboard / swarm: agents don't message each other directly — they read and write a shared scratchpad and react to whatever changed

slides.title: How Agents Actually Pass Context
slides.body: The coordination pattern only works if you also control what crosses the boundary between agents.
bullets: Message passing keeps each agent's context small and isolated, but needs an explicit contract for what gets forwarded and what gets dropped
Shared state (a blackboard) avoids re-sending the same context repeatedly, but risks two agents overwriting the same field without some form of locking

Most production systems compress a sub-agent's output before it returns to the orchestrator — a 200-token summary instead of the sub-agent's full 5,000-token transcript keeps the supervisor's own context lean

slides.title: Trading Overhead for Isolation

rows: Medium — orchestrator can become a bottleneck
High — one failed worker doesn't crash the others
Independent subtasks that can run in parallel
Low — one bad stage poisons everything downstream
Work with a natural linear sequence
Medium — depends on how state is locked
Open-ended exploration with no fixed order

slides.title: Worked Example: Automated Code Review
slides.body: A 15-file pull request, split by responsibility instead of handed to one agent whole.
bullets: A planner agent reads only the PR diff and file list (a small context) and outputs a checklist of what needs review
Each reviewer sub-agent gets exactly one file's diff plus its direct dependencies — never the whole repo
An aggregator agent merges every reviewer's findings, drops duplicates, and ranks the rest by severity before a human sees anything
Net effect: every sub-agent's context stays under roughly 2K tokens, instead of one agent juggling 15 files at once and losing track of earlier ones

slides.title: The Bill Comes Due in Tokens
slides.body: The isolation multi-agent systems buy you isn't free — it's paid for in tokens and new failure modes.
bullets: Every extra agent hop re-sends context — a 4-agent chain can easily cost several times the tokens of one well-scoped agent call for the same task
Errors compound across stages: if each agent is individually 90% reliable, a 4-stage pipeline's end-to-end reliability drifts well below that
Debugging gets harder — a wrong final answer could originate at any step, so you need per-agent tracing to find which one caused it
Don't reach for multi-agent when a single agent with a well-curated, short tool list already solves the task — extra agents are latency and cost, not a free accuracy boost

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Split agents by the shape of the work, not by habit: linear stages -> pipeline, independent parallel subtasks -> supervisor-worker, open-ended exploration -> blackboard
Every hop between agents costs tokens and is a new place for context to be lost or an error to compound
Compress what crosses agent boundaries — pass summaries back to the orchestrator, not full transcripts
Default to a single, well-scoped agent first; add more agents only once one context window or tool list is visibly overloaded

questions.prompt: What's the strongest signal that a task is ready to move from one agent to a multi-agent system?
options: The team wants to use a newer framework
A single agent's context window or tool list is visibly overloaded and its performance is degrading
Multi-agent systems are always faster than a single agent
The task involves more than one file
questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems trade cost and coordination overhead for isolation — that trade is only worth making once a single agent is genuinely struggling with too much context or too many tools, not by default.

questions.prompt: In a supervisor-worker pattern, what happens if one worker sub-agent fails?
options: The entire system crashes immediately, same as a pipeline
The orchestrator can typically continue routing to other workers, since failures are isolated to that one subtask
All other workers automatically retry the failed worker's task
The shared blackboard is wiped and every agent restarts
questions.explanation: Supervisor-worker's main advantage over a pipeline is failure isolation: because the orchestrator routes independent subtasks, one worker's failure doesn't automatically poison the others' results the way a bad stage does in a linear pipeline.

questions.prompt: Why does a 4-stage agent pipeline often end up far less reliable than any single stage in it?
options: Because pipelines always run out of memory
Because each stage's errors compound — even at 90% reliability per stage, end-to-end reliability drops well below 90% across four stages
Because pipelines cannot use tools
Because later stages always ignore earlier stages' output
questions.explanation: Reliability compounds multiplicatively across sequential stages, so small per-stage error rates add up fast — this is exactly why a bad stage early in a pipeline can quietly poison everything downstream.

posts.title: Model Quantization: Shrinking Weights Without Losing Accuracy
posts.subtitle: A model doesn't get smaller by deleting parameters — it gets smaller by describing each one with fewer bits.
posts.summary: Quantization stores each weight with fewer bits (int8, int4) instead of the fp16/fp32 a model trains in, cutting memory 2-4x with surprisingly little accuracy loss — but only if you protect the handful of weight channels that carry disproportionate signal. Methods like GPTQ and AWQ do exactly that, which is why a 70B model can run on a single GPU instead of a rack of them.

slides.title: Same Weights, Fewer Bits Per Number
slides.body: Quantization doesn't remove parameters or change the architecture — it changes how precisely each weight is stored, trading numeric precision for a much smaller memory footprint.

slides.title: A 70B Model Doesn't Fit Where You Want It To
slides.body: Training and inference default to 16-bit floats, and that precision has a direct memory cost.
bullets: fp16/bf16 weights cost 2 bytes per parameter — a 70B model is ~140GB of weights alone, before the KV cache or activations
That's more than a single 80GB H100 can hold, forcing multi-GPU serving just to load the weights
Even a 'small' 7B model at fp16 is ~14GB — too tight for a 16GB consumer GPU once you add context

slides.title: Store Each Weight in Fewer Bits
slides.body: Quantization maps a tensor's float range onto a small integer range using a scale (and often a zero-point), then stores integers instead of floats.
bullets: int8 = 1 byte/param → roughly half the fp16 footprint
int4 = 0.5 byte/param → roughly a quarter of the fp16 footprint
Dequantize on the fly during matmul (scale * int_value), so the model still computes in a higher-precision space where it matters

slides.title: Why Naive Rounding Breaks the Model
slides.body: Rounding every weight to the nearest int4 value uniformly wrecks accuracy, because a small set of 'salient' weight channels carries disproportionate influence on the output.
bullets: GPTQ: quantizes one column at a time, using approximate second-order (Hessian) information to adjust the remaining unquantized weights and cancel out the rounding error it just introduced

AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization): profiles activations on a small calibration set to find which weight channels matter most, then keeps those effectively higher-precision (via per-channel scaling) while quantizing the rest aggressively
Both need only a small calibration dataset, not retraining — this is 'post-training quantization' (PTQ)

slides.title: Precision vs. Footprint

rows: Training, and serving when memory isn't the bottleneck
Safe default speedup with minimal measured quality loss
Consumer-GPU / edge serving; small, measurable quality dip
Usually needs quantization-aware training to stay usable

slides.title: Worked Example: Fitting 7B on a Single Consumer GPU
slides.body: Same model, three precisions, one 24GB card.
bullets: fp16: ~14GB just for weights, leaving little room for KV cache — long-context prompts OOM
int8: ~7GB for weights, comfortably leaves headroom for a bigger KV cache and longer context
int4 (GGUF Q4_K_M via llama.cpp): ~4GB for weights, enough to run alongside other apps or serve a much longer context window on the same card

slides.title: When Quantization Isn't the Right Call
slides.body: The memory savings are real, but they aren't free.
bullets: Tasks needing precise numeric or multi-step exact reasoning (arithmetic, exact code output) are more sensitive to quantization error than open-ended text generation
Below 4-bit, quality tends to degrade sharply without quantization-aware training (QAT) — a 2-bit PTQ model can look fluent but be subtly wrong more often
Gains aren't guaranteed to transfer: always re-evaluate a quantized model on your own task/eval set, not just a generic perplexity number
Fine-tuning a quantized model directly is awkward — this is exactly why QLoRA fine-tunes small adapters in higher precision on top of frozen 4-bit weights instead

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Quantization changes numeric precision per weight, not parameter count or architecture
Naive uniform rounding fails because a small set of channels carries outsized influence — GPTQ and AWQ exist to protect exactly those
int8 is close to a free lunch; int4 is the sweet spot for consumer hardware; sub-4-bit usually needs QAT to stay usable
Always re-validate a quantized model on your actual task — generic benchmarks don't guarantee your use case survives the compression

questions.prompt: What does quantization actually change about a trained model?
options: The number of parameters in the model
The numeric precision (bit-width) used to store each weight
The model's architecture (layers, attention heads)
The tokenizer's vocabulary size
questions.explanation: Quantization keeps the same parameters and architecture — it just stores each weight with fewer bits (e.g. int4 instead of fp16), which is why it shrinks memory without retraining.

questions.prompt: Why do methods like AWQ deliberately protect a small subset of 'salient' weight channels instead of quantizing every weight the same way?
options: Because those channels are always located in the first layer of the network
Because a small number of channels, identified from activation statistics, carry disproportionate influence on the output — rounding them the same as everything else causes most of the accuracy loss
Because GPU hardware can only quantize even-numbered channels
Because it makes the resulting file format compatible with GGUF
questions.explanation: AWQ profiles activations on a calibration set to find which weight channels matter most for the outputs, then effectively keeps those higher-precision (via scaling) while quantizing the rest hard. Uniform rounding ignores this and loses much more accuracy for the same bit-width.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of pushing quantization to 2-bit without extra techniques like quantization-aware training (QAT)?
options: Inference becomes slower than running the full fp16 model
The model file becomes unreadable by any inference engine
Accuracy tends to degrade sharply — the model can stay fluent while being subtly wrong more often
The model loses the ability to run on GPUs entirely
questions.explanation: Below roughly 4-bit, post-training quantization alone usually isn't enough to preserve quality — errors compound and the model degrades noticeably unless it was trained (or fine-tuned) with quantization baked into the process, i.e. QAT.

posts.title: Agent Guardrails: Constraining a Tool-Using Model
posts.subtitle: Letting a model call tools is the easy part. Making sure it can't do something catastrophic is the hard part.
posts.summary: Giving an LLM tool access turns it from a text generator into an actor that can delete files, spend money, or send messages. Real guardrails are layered — allow-listing which tools exist, scoping what each call can touch, validating arguments before execution, and gating irreversible actions behind human confirmation — because any single layer can fail or be bypassed.

slides.title: Tool Access Turns a Chatbot Into an Actor
slides.body: A model that can only produce text can, at worst, say something wrong. A model wired to tools can delete a database, push to production, or wire money — the failure mode changes from 'wrong answer' to 'wrong action'.

slides.title: The Model Doesn't Actually Know What 'Safe' Means
slides.body: An LLM will confidently call whatever tool the context nudges it toward — including a destructive one — if it seems like the reasonable next step.
bullets: A coding agent told to 'clean up the repo' can interpret that as `rm -rf` on the wrong directory
A support agent with email access can be prompt-injected via a ticket's own text into sending data to an attacker-controlled address
The model has no innate sense of 'irreversible' — deleting a row and printing a summary look equally routine to it

slides.title: Four Layers of Guardrails
slides.body: No single layer is sufficient on its own — each stops a different class of mistake.
bullets: Allow-listing: only expose the specific tools the task needs, not every tool the server could offer
Scoping: parameterize what a tool CAN touch (e.g. a delete_file tool hard-restricted to a sandboxed directory)
Validation: inspect arguments before execution — schema checks, path traversal checks, dry-run diffs
Human-in-the-loop: require explicit confirmation before irreversible or high-blast-radius actions

slides.title: Worked Example: A Coding Agent With File Write Access
slides.body: Layering guardrails on a single tool call, in order:
bullets: Allow-list: agent gets write_file and run_tests, not execute_shell or send_http_request
Scoping: write_file rejects any path that resolves outside the repo root, even via '../' traversal
Validation: a diff is generated and checked against a max-lines-changed threshold before applying
Human-in-the-loop: git push --force or any change touching /prod config requires explicit user approval

slides.title: What Each Layer Stops — and Misses

rows: Misuse WITHIN an allowed tool's scope
A legitimately-scoped but still harmful call (e.g. deleting the right file at the wrong time)
A maliciously-plausible call that passes every schema check
Nothing structurally — but adds latency and invites rubber-stamping under fatigue

slides.title: Where a Guardrail Actually Holds
slides.body: Not all guardrails are equally enforceable — where you place one determines whether it can be bypassed.
bullets: Prompt-level instructions ('never delete production data') are advisory only — a prompt injection from tool output can override them
Middleware that intercepts every tool call BEFORE execution is enforceable code, not a suggestion the model can talk itself out of
Sandboxing (containers, read-only filesystems, restricted network egress) is the strongest layer — it holds even if every upstream layer is fooled

slides.title: When Guardrails Break the Agent
slides.body: Over-guarding has real costs, not just theoretical ones.
bullets: Too-narrow allow-lists make the agent unable to complete legitimate tasks, so users route around it with a broader, less-safe tool
Prompt-only guardrails create false confidence — they look like protection but a crafted tool-output injection walks right through them
Confirmation on EVERY action causes 'approval fatigue' — users start clicking 'approve' reflexively, defeating the point of the gate

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Treat guardrails as defense-in-depth, not a single checkbox — assume any one layer can fail
Enforce constraints in code that executes before the tool runs, not just in the system prompt
Reserve human confirmation for genuinely irreversible or high-blast-radius actions, or it stops working
Sandboxing is the layer that holds even when the model is actively fooled — invest there first

questions.prompt: Why is a prompt-level instruction like 'never delete production data' an unreliable guardrail on its own?
options: LLMs cannot read instructions longer than a few sentences
It's advisory only — text injected into the context (e.g. from a tool's own output) can override or distract from it
System prompts are ignored by every model
It only works for tool calls, not text generation
questions.explanation: A prompt-level rule lives in the same context the model reasons over, so it can be crowded out or contradicted by other text the model reads — including attacker-controlled tool output. Enforceable code that runs before execution doesn't have that weakness.

questions.prompt: A tool called delete_file is scoped to only operate inside /repo. What kind of mistake does this scoping NOT prevent?
options: Calling a tool that isn't on the allow-list
The agent legitimately deleting the right file inside /repo at the wrong, harmful time
SQL injection
Network timeouts
questions.explanation: Scoping restricts WHERE a tool can act, not WHETHER a given in-scope call is a good idea. A file inside /repo can still be the wrong one to delete right now — that's what validation and human confirmation are for.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of requiring human confirmation for every single tool call an agent makes?
options: It's technically impossible to implement
Users experience approval fatigue and start clicking 'approve' reflexively, which defeats the purpose of the gate
It makes the model less accurate
It violates the MCP specification
questions.explanation: Confirmation gates only work if humans actually read them. Gating everything trains users to click through without looking — reserve the gate for genuinely irreversible or high-blast-radius actions so it stays meaningful.

posts.title: MCP Resources: Context Without a Tool Call
posts.subtitle: Not everything a model needs has to be fetched through a function call — sometimes it's just attached.
posts.summary: MCP gives servers three distinct primitives — tools, resources, and prompts — and conflating them wastes tokens and round-trips. Resources are URI-addressed, read-only context that a client can list and attach directly, without asking the model to decide to fetch them via a tool call.

slides.title: MCP Has Three Primitives — Most Servers Only Use One
slides.body: Tools, Resources, and Prompts each answer a different question: what should the model DO, what should it SEE, and what should the user SAY. Treating them as interchangeable costs latency and reliability.

slides.title: Tools Are an Indirect Way to Say 'Here's Some Context'
slides.body: If a server exposes a 'read_file' tool just to hand the model a config file it always needs, that's an extra model decision, an extra round-trip, and a failure point if the model doesn't think to call it.
bullets: The model has to infer it SHOULD call the tool — it's not guaranteed to, especially with many tools competing for attention
Each tool call is a full request/response turn: added latency, added tokens for the call + result framing
Static context that never changes shouldn't depend on model judgment to appear at all

slides.title: Resources: URI-Addressed, Client-Attached Content
slides.body: A resource is identified by a URI (file:///path, postgres://schema, or any custom scheme a server defines) and exposed through three methods.
bullets: resources/list — server advertises what's available (URI, name, MIME type)
resources/read — client fetches the actual content for a given URI
resources/subscribe — client asks to be notified when a resource's content changes

slides.title: Tools vs. Resources vs. Prompts

rows: Take an action or fetch dynamic, parameterized data

slides.title: Worked Example: A Database MCP Server
slides.body: A server exposing a database can offer both a resource and a tool for very different jobs.
bullets: Resource schema://orders — the table schema, attached once at conversation start so the model always has it in context, no tool call needed
Tool query_database(sql) — the model decides WHEN and WHAT to query, since that's dynamic and parameterized
Using a tool for the schema too would mean the model might forget to fetch it before writing a query that references a nonexistent column

slides.title: Who Actually Decides What Gets Attached
slides.body: In most MCP clients, resource attachment is a client/user-driven UI action (e.g. an @-mention or file picker), not an autonomous model decision.
bullets: The user or client app chooses which resources enter context — predictable, auditable, no prompt-injection surface from a rogue 'attach this' instruction
Tools, by contrast, are offered to the model and it autonomously decides when to invoke them based on the conversation
This split is deliberate: it keeps read-only context deterministic while keeping actions flexible

slides.title: Where Resources Fall Short
slides.body: Resources solve the 'always-needed static context' problem, not every context problem.
bullets: Without subscribe, a resource can go stale — the client has to re-read it, the server won't push updates on its own
A server exposing thousands of URIs (e.g. every file in a repo) makes resources/list itself expensive to enumerate and browse
Resources return raw content, not a reasoned result — if you need the model to compute something over the data, that's still a tool's job

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Use a resource for context that's known upfront and doesn't require the model to decide to fetch it
Use a tool when the model needs to decide WHEN and WITH WHAT PARAMETERS to act
Subscribe to resources you expect to change mid-conversation — otherwise the model works off a stale snapshot
Don't build a 'get_config' tool when a resource does the same job with zero model-decision risk

questions.prompt: Why might static context (like a DB schema) be a poor fit for a tool call?
options: Tools can't return text content
The model might never decide to call the tool, and each call adds a full round-trip for something that never changes
Tools are always slower than resources at the network level
MCP doesn't allow tools to return schemas
questions.explanation: A tool call depends on the model deciding to invoke it. For context that should ALWAYS be present, attaching it as a resource guarantees it's there without relying on model judgment or spending a round-trip.

questions.prompt: Who typically decides which MCP resource gets attached to a conversation?
options: The model, autonomously, the same way it picks tools
The client/user, via an explicit action like an @-mention or file picker
It's chosen randomly by the server
It's fixed at server install time and can never change
questions.explanation: Resource attachment is deliberately client/user-driven, which keeps what enters context predictable and auditable — unlike tools, which the model invokes autonomously mid-conversation.

questions.prompt: A resource was read once at the start of a long conversation and the underlying data has since changed. What keeps the model's view fresh?
options: MCP automatically re-reads every resource every turn
Nothing by default — the client must use resources/subscribe or manually re-read to avoid a stale snapshot
The model detects staleness on its own
Resources can't be read more than once per session
questions.explanation: Without subscribing, a resource is a point-in-time snapshot. resources/subscribe lets the client get notified of changes so it knows to re-fetch, but that behavior isn't automatic.

posts.title: Circuit Breakers: Stopping One Failure From Spreading
posts.subtitle: A wrapped call that trips open before a dying dependency drags everything down with it.
posts.summary: A circuit breaker wraps a risky call and trips 'open' after too many failures, so a struggling dependency fails fast instead of dragging the whole system down with slow timeouts and thread exhaustion. It recovers by testing the dependency with a trickle of traffic in a 'half-open' state before fully closing again.

slides.title: One Slow Dependency Can Take Down Everything Upstream
slides.body: When a downstream service starts timing out instead of failing fast, every caller piles up waiting threads — and the outage spreads backward through the whole call graph.

slides.title: Retries and Timeouts Alone Make It Worse
slides.body: A naive client retries a failing call and waits out the full timeout each time. Under load, that multiplies traffic to an already-struggling service.
bullets: A 5s timeout x 3 retries = 15s a thread sits blocked on one bad call
Thread pools of 50-200 workers exhaust in seconds once every caller is stuck waiting
Once callers queue up, the failure spreads to services that depend on THEM

slides.title: Three States: Closed, Open, Half-Open
slides.body: A circuit breaker sits in front of a risky call and tracks its recent success rate, switching behavior based on what it sees.
bullets: Closed: calls pass through normally; failures are counted in a rolling window
Open: once failures cross a threshold, every call fails immediately (no network hop) for a cooldown period
Half-open: after the cooldown, a small number of test calls are let through to see if the dependency recovered

slides.title: Worked Example: A Payment Service Call
slides.body: resilience4j-style config: trip the breaker if 50% of the last 20 calls fail, stay open 30 seconds, then allow 5 trial calls in half-open.
bullets: Calls 1-20: 11 failures (55%) → breaker trips OPEN at call 20
Calls 21-∞ for 30s: rejected instantly with a fallback (e.g. 'try again shortly'), no network call made
At 30s: breaker goes HALF-OPEN, lets 5 calls through — if ≥50% still fail, it re-opens for another 30s; if they succeed, it closes

slides.title: Circuit Breaker vs. Its Neighbors
slides.body: These patterns solve different problems and are usually combined, not chosen between.

rows: Caps how long ONE call can block
Re-attempts a single failed call, hoping it was transient
Stops attempting calls after a failure pattern, fails fast instead
Isolates resource pools so one dependency can't starve others

slides.title: Where the Breaker Lives
slides.body: Two dominant approaches, with a real tradeoff between them.
bullets: In-process library (resilience4j, Polly, Hystrix-successor patterns): per-call-site control, but every service must implement it consistently
Sidecar / service mesh (Envoy, Istio, Linkerd): centralized, language-agnostic, applied uniformly — but tuning is coarser and less code-aware
Most production stacks use the mesh for network-level protection and a library for business-logic-aware fallbacks

slides.title: When a Breaker Hurts More Than It Helps
slides.body: Breakers are not free — badly tuned ones create new failure modes.
bullets: Low-traffic services: a 'last 20 calls' window can trip on 11 unlucky requests spread over an hour, not a real outage
Global breakers: one breaker for a whole service (not per-endpoint) can block a healthy endpoint because a different one is failing
Thundering herd on recovery: if every client's half-open trial fires at the same instant, the recovering service gets slammed again — stagger trial timing

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A circuit breaker trades a slow failure for a fast, cheap one — that's the entire point
Tune the failure threshold and window size to real traffic volume, not a copy-pasted default
Always pair it with a fallback response; failing fast is only useful if the caller can do something with 'no' immediately
Scope breakers per-dependency (ideally per-endpoint), never one global breaker for a whole service

questions.prompt: Why does a circuit breaker fail calls immediately instead of retrying when it's OPEN?
options: Retrying is against the HTTP spec
To stop adding load to an already-struggling dependency and free up caller threads instantly
Because open connections cost more money
It's a bug in most implementations
questions.explanation: The whole point of tripping open is to stop sending traffic to a dependency that's already failing, and to return control to the caller immediately instead of tying up a thread for the full timeout.

questions.prompt: What does the HALF-OPEN state test?
options: Whether the client's network connection is stable
Whether the dependency has recovered, using a small trial of live traffic before fully re-opening the floodgates
Whether the load balancer needs to be restarted
The current CPU usage of the caller
questions.explanation: Half-open lets a limited number of real calls through as a probe. If they mostly succeed, the breaker closes; if they still fail, it re-opens for another cooldown period.

questions.prompt: A single circuit breaker wraps ALL calls to a payment service, which has 5 different endpoints. One endpoint (refunds) starts failing. What happens?
options: Only the refunds endpoint gets blocked, others unaffected
Nothing — breakers only track network-level errors
The breaker trips for the whole service, blocking healthy endpoints like 'charge' too — a common tuning mistake
The breaker automatically splits itself per endpoint
questions.explanation: A breaker scoped too broadly punishes healthy traffic for an unrelated failure. Scoping breakers per-endpoint (or per logical operation) avoids this collateral damage.

posts.title: Structured Outputs: Forcing an LLM to Always Emit Valid JSON
posts.subtitle: Prompting for JSON gets you close most of the time. Constrained decoding gets you a parser that never fails.
posts.summary: Asking a model nicely to 'return JSON' still leaves room for trailing commas, wrapped markdown fences, or a field that silently drifts from your schema. Constrained (grammar-guided) decoding fixes this at the token level: the schema is compiled into a finite-state machine, and at every generation step the sampler masks out any token that would violate it. The output is syntactically guaranteed to match the schema — though not guaranteed to be semantically correct.

slides.title: "Return Only JSON" Is a Request, Not a Guarantee
bullets: Prompt-only JSON mode: the model is free to generate any token — it just usually chooses valid ones
Constrained decoding: the sampler is mechanically forbidden from generating an invalid token in the first place
The difference matters most at scale — a 1-in-200 parse failure is a shrug in a demo and a paging alert in production

slides.title: Free-Form Generation Breaks Downstream Parsers
slides.body: An LLM samples one token at a time from a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary. Nothing about that process knows what 'valid JSON' means.
bullets: Common failures: a trailing comma, an unescaped quote inside a string, ```json fences wrapped around the object, a numeric field returned as "42" instead of 42
Few-shot examples and 'you MUST return valid JSON' instructions reduce failures but don't eliminate them — the model can still drift under an unusual input
Retrying on parse failure adds latency and cost, and still isn't a guarantee — you're just resampling from the same imperfect distribution
Nested optional fields and enums are where prompting fails hardest: the model has to remember every allowed value with no structural help

slides.title: Compile the Schema Into a Grammar, Then Mask Tokens
slides.body: Constrained decoding moves validity out of the prompt and into the sampler itself.
bullets: Step 1: compile the JSON Schema (or a regex, or a context-free grammar) into a finite-state machine — one state per valid position in the structure
Step 2: before each token is sampled, compute which tokens are legal transitions from the current state
Step 3: set the logits of every illegal token to −∞ (mask them out), then sample normally from what remains
Step 4: advance the FSM state by whichever token was chosen, repeat until the schema reaches an accepting state
The model never 'chooses' to break the schema — an invalid token simply has zero probability of being picked

slides.title: Where the FSM Lives in the Serving Stack
slides.body: This runs inside the inference server, on the same forward pass — it isn't a separate validation step after generation.
bullets: Libraries: Outlines, NVIDIA's XGrammar, and llama.cpp's GBNF grammars all implement this pattern; vLLM and TGI expose it as 'guided decoding'
Per-token mask computation has to be fast — XGrammar-style engines precompute most of the FSM transition table so masking adds low single-digit-percent overhead, not a second forward pass
Regex and simple grammars compile in milliseconds; deeply nested schemas with many optional branches take longer to compile and can blow up FSM state count
Because masking happens at the logits, it composes with normal sampling (temperature, top-p) — you still get output diversity within the allowed structure

slides.title: Three Ways to Get JSON Out of a Model
slides.body: Each rung trades effort and flexibility for a stronger guarantee.

rows: Not addressed — still a separate problem

slides.title: Example: Extracting a Support Ticket Into a Fixed Schema
slides.body: Schema: { "priority": "low"|"medium"|"high", "category": string, "needs_escalation": boolean }
bullets: Prompt-only: on an ambiguous ticket the model sometimes writes "priority": "High" (wrong case) or omits needs_escalation entirely — both break a strict parser

With constrained decoding: after generating '"priority": "', the FSM only allows the tokens that spell low, medium, or high followed by a closing quote — capitalization drift and hallucinated categories become structurally impossible
The FSM still can't stop the model from picking the wrong enum value for the wrong reason — it guarantees the field is one of the three strings, not that it's the correct one
This is why teams pair constrained decoding with eval sets that check semantic accuracy, not just parse success

slides.title: Where It Falls Short — and When to Skip It
slides.body: Constrained decoding solves syntax, not meaning, and it isn't free.
bullets: It cannot fix hallucinated content — a perfectly-shaped JSON object can still contain a fabricated field value
Overly rigid grammars can hurt quality: forcing a specific field order or an unnatural schema can make the model 'fight' the constraint and produce worse content within the valid shape
Very large or deeply recursive schemas increase FSM compile time and memory — not a good fit for schemas that change on every request
If you just need a rough structure for a low-stakes internal tool, prompting plus a lenient JSON parser (like handling trailing commas) is often good enough and much simpler

Constrained decoding is table stakes when a downstream system will crash or silently corrupt data on a malformed field — agent tool-calling, structured data pipelines, anything machine-parsed with no human in the loop

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Prompting for JSON is probabilistic; constrained decoding is structural — it masks illegal tokens so the output can't leave the schema
The mechanism: compile the schema to a finite-state machine, mask logits at every step, advance the FSM as tokens are chosen
It guarantees syntax, never semantics — a valid-shaped object can still be factually wrong, so you still need accuracy evals
Reach for it whenever a machine, not a human, is the one reading the output — agent tool calls, extraction pipelines, anything a parser crash would break

questions.prompt: What does constrained (grammar-guided) decoding actually change about generation?
options: It runs the model twice and picks the better output
It masks the logits of tokens that would violate the schema, so only legal tokens can be sampled
It fine-tunes the model on JSON examples before serving
It asks a second, smaller model to validate the output after generation
questions.explanation: The schema is compiled into a finite-state machine; at each step, illegal tokens get their logits set to −∞ before sampling, so an invalid token can never be chosen in the first place.

questions.prompt: A ticket-extraction pipeline using constrained decoding returns { "priority": "high", "category": "refund", "needs_escalation": true } for a ticket that's actually about a login bug. What does this tell you?
options: Constrained decoding failed — this should be impossible
The schema was compiled incorrectly
The output is syntactically valid but semantically wrong — constrained decoding never guaranteed content accuracy
The FSM needs a larger vocabulary
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding only guarantees the output matches the schema's shape and allowed values. It has no mechanism to check whether 'refund' is the factually correct category — that's a separate accuracy problem, checked with evals.

questions.prompt: When is prompt-only JSON generation (no constrained decoding) the more sensible choice?
options: Whenever an autonomous agent will parse the output with no human review
Whenever the schema is simple, the stakes are low, and a lenient parser can absorb minor formatting slips
Whenever the schema has strict enums that must never be wrong
Never — constrained decoding has no real downsides
questions.explanation: Constrained decoding adds setup cost (compiling a grammar) and can slightly constrain output quality on rigid schemas. For low-stakes, simple-schema cases where a forgiving parser is fine, plain prompting is simpler and often sufficient.
